Runner-up, Fiction:
Brian Stevens, “A Hairy Tale”

“The hair was another animal entirely.” Funny, dark, surreal, and completely surprising: “A Hairy Tale” by Brian Stevens follows the weird life of the narrator’s cellmate’s hair. It is also deeply strange, in the best possible way.

–Elizabeth McCracken

A Hairy Tale
by Brian Stevens

My celly’s hair is a nightmare. The stuff just goes everywhere. Every morning, my first chore is to wipe all his hair off the floor. I clean the cell to no avail.

***

Ants occupied the cell when I first arrived. They crawled in through the cracks and marched along the walls. Any food or flesh that crossed their paths was quickly devoured. Their bites would leave itchy red welts on my hands and feet. I fought them tooth and nail with everything I had: baby powder, soap, shampoo, laundry detergent, bleach. I was able to slow them down; as summer ended, the weather cooled and they eventually went away. Then, only the hair remained.

***

The hair was another animal together, but unlike the ants, it could not be contained. The fans in the cell created tornadoes of tangles that clung to anything they touched. There was hair on my bed; my clothes; in my mouth and nose; my coffee when I took a drink; and the drain when I used the sink. Hair came back around, got stuck in the fans, and when I rinsed my washcloth, hair stuck to my hands. The hair began to take on a life of its own: no matter how much I cleaned, I was never alone.

The hairs were long, black, and curly like the pubes of a buffalo. Bundles of them would roll across the ground like tumbleweeds blowing in the wind of the Wild West. Sometimes, I would mistake a stray strand for a cockroach as it scurried from one side of the cell to the other. Hairs strung along the shelves like broken spiderwebs in abandoned basements. The black hairs were bad, but the white ones were worse: they were invisible to the naked eye and could hide in plain sight. They were ghosts of dead hairs past that would continue to haunt me for eternity. Something drastic had to be done.

***

No ordinary razor would ever be able to chop down that forest of frizz. I searched for some scissors but had to settle for a shank—a dirty guy named Sanchez sold it to me for six soups and seven shots of coffee. He told me it was so sharp, it could slit a pig’s throat with a single slice. I took his word and kept it carefully wrapped in a johnny sack. I certainly did not want to get caught with such a serious piece of contraband, so I had to act soon.

That night, I asked my celly to cut his hair; he refused. He knew it made a mess everyday but didn’t seem very concerned about cleaning it up. He was also deeply religious and claimed his hair gave him strength like Samson.

As he drank himself to sleep, I thought about cutting some of his hair but then decided it all needed to be shaved. Upon further inspection, I realized: even with a shaved head, his hair would still grow back, and that would never do. No, his whole head would have to come off.

First place, Nonfiction:
Deanna Carney, “Sit. Stay.”

In a few short pages, Deanna Carney’s wonderfully written “Sit. Stay.” manages to look at a whole life and contemplates death and love and no less than the nature of time, all through the animals that the narrator has known since childhood. It is full of beauty and sadness and the paradox of loving animals when the human world is too much.

–Elizabeth McCracken

Sit. Stay.
by Deanna Carney

Seven cats shared our cramped apartment in Virginia.

Family lore fills in false memories: a pungent cloud of clumped kitty litter, discarded beer bottles, marijuana, my soiled diapers.

Did my biological father’s heroin addiction have a smell?

***

A tomcat, Rocky, was the most beloved; his memory enshrined in poetry I inherited two decades later, after my father’s heroin overdose. In hindsight, the name seems to be a foreshadowing.

I had to be younger than two. Momma hadn’t yet escaped quickly to Texas, her skin a carry-on bag full of storm-hued bruises. She hadn’t been ejected from the seat and flown through the windshield of a car. She hadn’t died, leaving my father with nothing more than memories and cats.

***

In Texas, my Nannie and her new husband fed, clothed, and put me to bed after Momma died. Well, they must have, because I survived. And there was no one else to do it; at least, no one wanted to, as Nannie would later frequently remind me.

Someone gave me a puppy: a pile of ebony fluff we named Blackie. He stayed in the add-on room that housed the water softener. While he bathed me in the perfume of puppy breath, I licked fallen rock salt pellets meant to condition the hard Hill Country water running through pipes beneath our single-wide trailer.

One day, while I dipped my fingers in a bucket of sudsy water Nannie was using to wash our little brown truck, my puppy ran away. I cried all the salt from my body as Nannie and I called out for him, our two-person search party scouting the neighborhood in vain.

I had to be younger than four—I still slept in the room that I used to share with Momma; my toys were still in the closet where her clothes used to be.

***

I wore a dress and socks with lace the day Nannie and her husband became my new mom and dad. The man behind the desk, making it legal, seemed much like the Wizard of Oz. We went to a lot, picked out a double-wide that had a bowl of fake fruit displayed in the kitchen.

Dad brought me a dachshund the color of a dried bloodstain—his name was Mister. Barrel-bodied and surefooted, Mister was not adorably mini-sized: at the end of a leash, he may as well have been a trained sled dog. Any attempt to walk him ended with me dragged across the asphalt behind his drumstick legs.

Unable to bear my tears, Dad rehomed Mister. I begged for a sibling. Instead, Mom and I went to pick out a puppy from an apricot-colored patch of poodles. I named him Danny Boy, undoubtedly under Mom’s influence. Many nights, I carried Danny Boy to bed with me, only to wake up and find him in Mom’s room. From day one, that dog was decidedly hers.

I must have been younger than five. I hadn’t graduated from kindergarten yet. Dad hadn’t been crushed behind the steering wheel of an eighteen-wheeler. Mom hadn’t gone to a hospital in Missouri and returned without him. Loving her hadn’t become painful. Years passed between us alone in that house. Silence, anger, tears.

***

Walking home from the bus stop one fall afternoon, I heard a kitten’s pleading cry beneath a garbage can. I took him home; bathed his long tabby fur; begged to keep him; and named him Tigea. Eventually, I taught him to walk on a leash.

I was younger than fifteen. I hadn’t found out I was pregnant. I hadn’t run away with my much older boyfriend. I hadn’t felt fear and bravery swirl inside me. I wasn’t yet married. I wasn’t yet an adult.

***

We found a German shepherd mix with floppy ears and named him Bogie: where our first daughter was born. In the next five years, we had a second daughter; then, a son. I had never known love as deep as what my heart held for them. Life was giggles and tiny toes.

I was younger than twenty-one. I was still able to kiss my children before bed, every night. My heart still knew happiness. I wasn’t yet divorced. My children weren’t kept from me. I hadn’t begun drinking.

***

At a gas station, I was offered a tiny red pup: the last of a litter, the runt no one wanted. I named her Lexi.

I taught her to sit, shake, and lay down. We went to parks and swam in rivers. I curled on the floor next to her, crying tears onto her copper coat when she died in the living room.

I was younger than thirty-nine. I hadn’t learned the full consequence of surrendering my heart to someone who would help me destroy it. Or how my attempt to drown the world hurt anyone, other than myself. I hadn’t noticed how far I had traveled from God or begun my eight-year sentence for DUI.

***

I am years away from the broken heart and mind that brought me here; months away from the freedom of open skies and second chances. I have had time to be still with my past and make peace with its voice. I’ve found support. I know love.

One day, when my foundation is fully formed on the other side of this fence, I will get another dog, confident that no matter what comes, I have: the strength to sit, and the peace to stay through it, even when it rains—

like cats and dogs

Runner-up, Nonfiction:
Matthew Mendoza, “Zen and the Art of Civil Commitment”

“Zen and the Art of Civil Commitment” is a clear-eyed essay describing, with precision, elegance, and even dark humor, taking a questionnaire that begins the process of civil commitment, the Kafka-esque practice of keeping sex offenders incarcerated after their sentences are served. It is also, without sentiment, falsity, or self-importance, about looking for redemption inside of prison through both words and deeds, art, and other people.

–Elizabeth McCracken

Zen and the Art of Civil Commitment
by Matthew Mendoza

Yesterday, I was called to the Unit Education Building for a psychological exam. There, the proxy informed me the State of Texas selected me for the Civil Commitment Process. I floated outside my body. The proxy gave me a blue pencil, a test booklet, and a scantron for my answers.

***

Generally speaking, The Civil Commitment Process is designed to catch “Predators with Behavioral Abnormalities”—the psychological exam is the beginning of that process. Failing the exam or refusing to take it is proof of the need for civil commitment.

Of course, I took it. I answered questions like: Do you ever feel like a soulless husk? Does your eyesight come and go? Is high jumping your favorite sport?

***

Texas inmates are excluded from many things involving the legal system: child support, civil proceedings, divorces, and property seizures can all be commenced without the inmate present. But that’s not all: an inmate may not even be notified until after the judgement. (An interesting side note: a Texas inmate can’t interact with the parole board, unless they hire an attorney.)

Civil commitment is a little different but not much: it circumvents the Constitution, claiming to be a public safety or civil proceeding instead of a criminal one—even though the result is the same. The difference is: the state must provide evidence an inmate is an immediate, continual threat upon release. The psychological exam is part of the state’s case.

***

A lot of the questions, including those three, repeated in some form or another. About a dozen times. As I answered and re-answered the questions, I wondered if consistency was the metric. I wondered if there was an overlay, a graph that could show change. I wondered if there is something metaphysical about certain sports; if so, I would add breakdancing and fishing to the list.

I just don’t know how you calculate points for contemplation or joy, if winning is the only metric.

***

I committed a horrible crime. It was inexcusable. I hurt my victim. I destroyed the respect and trust of the people I love forever.

As bad as that is, it isn’t all. During my first years of prison, I was on both sides of every single, fucked up thing one person can do to another. Part of it was survival; part of it was anger. Regardless, all of it was wrong—and none of it I can ever make right.

I have no desire to do crime nor break even the most mundane laws. I don’t care if I ever leave prison. A free-world sex offender has little value. (You don’t want a sex offender as a co-worker or a neighbor, so save the pep talk. Besides, that’s not what this is.) Life after prison is punitive; in prison, no one pretends otherwise.

I don’t care about dope prison politics or “The Price is Right.” In the eyes of the administration and most inmates, that makes me a mystery—and a mystery means: I’m not a very good inmate.

There is nothing mysterious about the things I care about: reading and writing, collecting all the playwrights in the Library of America book series, the awards and honors I’ve received despite being in prison. I care about finding a way to redeem myself.

***

I am the Assistant Program Coordinator for the assisted living dorm in my unit. Part of what I do is help inmates with disabilities and mobility issues. Sometimes, I help these men get and stay sober. I celebrate their recoveries—from medical events or their addictions—with cakes, coffee, and movies. Sometimes, if someone proves they can stay sober, I help pay off their drug debts. I do all of this out of my own locker. Most of the money comes from awards and stipends I’ve earned as a writer.

I think redemption, like faith, is personal.

In prison, I have value: as a writer and a teacher, even if it is an incredibly flawed system. My eyesight and my ideas about sports aside, I am content with the world I’ve created for myself in this community.

I feel fulfilled: a step on a journey towards peace.

*

Runner-up, Nonfiction:
Steven Perez, “Aunt Terry and Josiah King”

In “Aunt Terry and Josiah King,” Steven Perez writes beautifully and wrenchingly about the deep pain and separation from those he loves—his dying aunt, his pregnant daughter—and about looking for impossible consolation in what he’s left with. The people in this essay are so well drawn they will break your heart.

–Elizabeth McCracken

Aunt Terry and Josiah King
by Steven Perez

My mother’s sister was on her deathbed. A surgeon had cut her open, gutted her. He was supposed to cut out scar tissue from two surgeries she had thirty years earlier; parts of her intestines were not properly digesting food. But he didn’t cut out enough of the bad intestines, and she didn’t wanna go through another surgery.

I called my mother at five-thirty in the morning. “She’s already passing,” she said. “It might be her last day.”

***

My daughter was six months pregnant. She was living with her baby’s father in a garage apartment with one bedroom, a kitchenette, and a restroom with a stand-up shower. The baby’s paternal grandfather had given them an old three-bedroom house. But the house was too rundown to live in.

My daughter applied for Section 8 housing aid. While she waited for assistance, her baby’s father worked on the house, but he didn’t have any money for the materials—he had been recently diagnosed with schizophrenia. The doctor said he couldn’t work until he got better.

My daughter worked nights at Wienerschnitzel. She had spent the last four years hooked on meth, in and outta jail, and then had been completely off the meth for five months—since the day she found out she was pregnant. She was twenty-five. My only child.

The child in her womb was a boy. My first grandchild.

***

My daughter, my mother, and her sister lived on the Gulf Coast in Corpus Christi, Texas: eighty-five miles southeast from where I lived in prison. I was locked up at the Connally Unit, a maximum-security prison in South Texas. It was January 9th, 2026. I had been locked up for the last nineteen years, eleven more to go before I was eligible for parole.

I lived in a warehouse dorm, where ten-by-five-foot, one-man cubicles were racked together by the dozens. Inmates in white—most of us Black or brown—were scattered throughout the dorm in and out of our cubicles. Some of us sat on benches in the center of the dorm, watching ESPN highlights of Houston Texan games; others watched ABC News on another TV, where an ICE agent gunned down a white woman in her SUV.

I stood up from my cubicle: two charcoal-colored, synthetic wool blankets folded together, making four. A linen sheet. Plastic mattress on an iron bunk. A stack of books on the floor: Scoot McCloud’s Understanding Comics, Volume IV of Peter Kreeft’s Socrates’ Children, The Georgia Review, Susan Wise Bauer’s The Well Educated Mind, and Alec Karakatsanis’s Copaganda. On the desk: a breviary, a black plastic rosary, a tablet, and ear buds.

***

On my way to the schoolhouse, guys from 4 Building—a  three-story-high square concrete building—hollered at me from behind the metal grating of their cell windows. Razor wire fences separated me from them.

“Tell ’em to get us outta here!” They said. “Theres no officers in the building. No rover to open our doors. No laws in the control picket. We’re trying to go to school.”

“All right,” I said. “I gotchu.”

Daylight had barely broken. The air was foggy and thick. I saw a wooden windmill covered in blue and yellow morning glories. I said to myself: They give glory to God through their beauty.

I sat alone in the middle of a classroom, surrounded by wooden tables and white, plastic chairs. In front of me, a chalkboard on a turquoise wall with four questions:

What are some ways to analyze a story?

What makes a good story?

Why should books be banned?

What stories should be allowed in the classroom?

The wall to my right wasn’t a wall at all; it was shatterproof glass. The sun revealed himself. I saw, outside the glass, two more concrete buildings; one was 8 Building, with cell numbers on the side underneath the windows: 72, 64, 56, 69, 61, 53. The other building a gym—no windows.

My worktable was full of papers, envelopes, and folders; drafts of handwritten prison memoirs; carbon copies of typewritten drafts already submitted for publication; packets of lit mag info; submission guidelines; a Poets & Writers magazine; an update from Malcom, a writer at PEN America; my tablet; and my earbuds.

I needed to write. I needed a shot of coffee. I needed to call my mother and check on my aunt.

I called my mother.

“I’m at the nursing home,” she said. “I stepped outside of the room, so I can talk to you. Her feet are red. The blood’s not circulating to her feet. I googled it. Means she has only about forty-eight hours left. The nurse bathed her. When she turned her on her side, she reached for the handrail on the side of the bed, but it wasn’t there. She was moved to another room with a different bed. She can still hear, though. The hearing is the last thing to go. I put music on for her. You wanna talk to her?”

“Yes. I do.”

She put the phone next to her ear.

“Hi, Tía,” I said. “I just called to say I love you with all my heart. I’m praying for you. We’ll be together one day.”

***

A few days earlier, she asked me: “Son, are they ever gonna let you outta there?”

“Yes, Tía. They’re gonna send me to school. And when I finish, they’re gonna let me outta here.”

“Steven, I had a dream. You were standing in front of me with your hands handcuffed behind your back. Then, they took the handcuffs off.” She sang me a song from Stevie Wonder: I just called . . . to say . . . I love you . . . And I mean it, from the bottom of my heart.

***

After we hung up, I opened up my tablet gallery app to a recent picture of her and my mother. My aunt was sitting at a round, wooden table with her left hand wrapped around a styrofoam Wienerschitzel cup on the table; her right hand rested above her stomach. She was wearing a pink short-sleeved blouse with white and black polka dots, a closed-lipped smile. The short distance between her nose and her chin revealed she wasn’t wearing her dentures. Her nose  was pointy, her cheeks chubby, and she had black and gray hair with a receding hairline. On the table sat a paper boat with what looked like a piece of deep-fried apple pie with smashed up gum bites. My mother was standing beside my aunt, her left arm resting around the back of my aunt’s neck and shoulders. Leaning on her and wrapping her body around her, almost smothering. My mother was wearing a lavender blouse with a black skirt. Her hair was brown, her eyebrows thins. Her broken nose that never healed right. She was looking down at the dessert tray. Her left cheek resting on the right side of my aunt’s head.

A painting of the Last Supper hung on the wall behind them.

I hadn’t been able to hold my aunt for almost two decades. Would she even recognize me with a taper fade, a face full of black and white reaching for my chest? She was too sick to visit. My life was tied up in electric razor-wire fences and smothered in concrete.

***

During our creative writing workshop, a discussion ensued: the difference between creating literary art for its own sake and creating literary art for publication and a paycheck.

Our facilitator, Mr. Hayes—a white guy with a red mustache and a six-day beard, who stooped his head to walk through the doorway, wearing a blue plaid cowboy shirt with pearl buttons—said publication was something he never really cared about. “I’m more interested in producing good art,” he said. “It’s not about the money or publication.” I thought about Kafka.

In Mr. Haye’s mind, we could spend the next ten years on a five-thousand-word essay and still not finish. In my mind, I was like, yes, we need to stay focused, determined in producing literary art for its own sake.

At the same time, most of our families are living in poverty. Our children and grandchildren need a home they call their own. They need a college education. We need to pay lawyers to get us outta here. And we need to build our own portfolios: so the free world can see we’re not the monsters the state’s lawyers said we were.

It’s easy to say it’s not about the money or publication when you and your families’ lives don’t depend on your writing.

***

By eight o’clock, that night, I was lying in my bunk, praying a rosary for my aunt. My mother was at home, getting ready to go back to the nursing home.

I woke up at six in the morning and lay in my bunk, fingering rosary beads while reciting Our Fathers, Hail Marys, and Glory Be’s. For breakfast I had a pouch of Vienna sausages and a generic chocolate protein shake poured over a bowl of generic Cinnamon Toast Crunch. An awful smell of mildew lingered in the air.

I remembered my Aunt Terry in the kitchen cooking scrambled eggs mixed with potatoes, pork chops in salsa, and refried beans. The smell of homemade flour tortillas on the comal.

I sat at my desk in the bunk, staring at a pencil draft of thoughts on sheets of college-ruled paper. At ten o’clock in the morning, I called my mother.

“She’s gone, son. She passed away last night, at nine-fifteen. She was glowing, in bed. The Lord took her.”

My mother’s only sister. Her last remaining sibling.

I sat and listened to my mother weep. “She’s not suffering anymore, Mom. She’s with the Lord. And God is now giving you a grandson.”

“You’re right, son. They say that for every person who dies, another is born. She wants to name him Josiah King.”

*

Biographies

Elizabeth McCracken is the author of nine books of fiction and nonfiction, including her most recent book, A Long Game. She was the winner of the 2014 Story Prize for Thunderstruck and Other Stories and has been a finalist for the National Book Award. Her stories have won three Pushcart Prizes, two National Magazine Awards, and have appeared in five editions of The Best American Short Stories. She taught fiction at The University of Texas at Austin where she held the title of the James A. Michener Chair in Fiction. She retired in May 2026 after 35 years of teaching and moved to England with her family.

Charles Hill is a writer in Texas.

Brian Stevens is a writer in his third year of the Pen City Writers class and is located in the Connally Unit Texas State Prison.

Deanna Carney is a writer and a recipient of the 2025 American Short Fiction Insider Prize in fiction for “Breach.” Hailing from San Antonio, Texas, Deanna is a proud mother of three and an excitable introvert. For her, writing is a shared connection to parents she lost too soon: a way to share, speak out, and love.

Matthew Mendoza is a playwright and poet who dabbles in fiction and nonfiction. His first book of poems, DIY Prison Project, was published in 2025 by Evening Street Press. Since 2018, his plays have been produced as podcasts and performed at festivals throughout the country. What’s Prison Like? was a 27th Annual Webby Award honoree in the Crime & Justice category.

Steven Perez is a fellow of the University of Texas at Austin English Department. He’s been studying creative writing under the author and professor Deb Olin Unferth for nine years. He’s a member of the Pen City Writers. He’s assigned to the Connally Unit maximum security prison in Kenedy, Texas. He’s currently awaiting transfer to earn a BA degree and an MA degree in humanities at the University of Houston Clear Lake. He was the 2025 American Short Fiction Insider Prize Runner-up in Nonfiction for “The Life and Mind of the Prisoner.”

Sergio Muro is a writer from Laredo, Texas. He is a Senior Editor and the Insider Prize Director at American Short Fiction and an editor for El Alboroto at The Rumpus. Sergio is at work on a short story collection centered around the Mexican diaspora.

item.title: The Literary Agent Who Lost the Narrative Thread
item.content:encoded:
As a literary agent, I’ve spent years shaping the stories of other people’s grief. There was the Pulitzer-nominated journalist who’d lost her only child when he was seven. And the Black descendent of Thomas Jefferson who, upon her father’s death, finally took the stories of his lineage seriously. Then there was the New York Times bestselling author who cared for young animals only to have to euthanize them when the time came.

Over the years, I’d built a business around refining narratives of heartbreak to reveal stories of earned strength. Yet, in the midst of my own grief story, I was cracking.

Literally.

It was months after my mother’s senseless death in a car accident, and I was at the dentist again. A part of me felt like Veda Sultenfuss from My Girl, with that invisible chicken bone down her throat. But I was sure: my tooth was cracking.

The book was replete with metaphors about the healing power of nature and the way that plants adapt to change due to the natural cycles of life and death.

The dentist was skeptical at first, but soon after “taking a look,” admitted that my molar had indeed cracked down to the gumline. He’d seal it, and we’d hope the bonding held.

“How long will it last?” I asked.

“Maybe months. Maybe forever,” the dentist said. “We cannot know.”

This felt too on the nose, like a metaphor I’d have edited out of someone else’s book.

I earned my publishing stripes representing heavy-hitting works of narrative nonfiction—the kinds of books that went on to be New York Times Editors’ Picks and that were nominated for prestigious awards. Only now, every time I tried to read nonfiction, I felt sick.

Each time I opened another book proposal, intent on doing what I’d always done—using the skills I’d acquired as a PhD student in Logic and Philosophy of Science to interrogate the core argument—the words on the page blurred together. Those big ideas, which had once helped me make sense of life’s complexity, allowing me to reframe my own story into one of triumph, now felt irrelevant, like I’d opened a book written in a language that had no frame of reference in my world.

I needed to get back to doing my job. I needed my teeth to stop breaking. I needed to find my footing. But what I really needed, I decided, was what I’d provided so many of my authors: a narrative to reframe loss into something that made sense.

I took over a month off from work. I spent time with my husband and my two young kids, and I wrote.

I wrote sad essays, which never found their narrative thrust. I wrote letters to my mom, which stumbled through bouts of melancholy before I finally admitted there was no plot. I wrote emails I never sent and emails I did send, but no line I ever cast managed to reel in anything healing.

So I decided to write something different, a book unlike anything that, at that time, I would have represented. I wrote fantasy.

The book was replete with metaphors about the healing power of nature and the way that plants adapt to change due to the natural cycles of life and death. It was a perfectly contained story, with every narrative thread tied up in a neat bow, showing how one could use grief as a portal to access true strength.

At long last, I’d created a narrative that oriented me within my own story.

“Have you thought about therapy?” the doctor asked gently.

I was overcome with relief. With those two simple words, this chapter of my life was finally over:

THE END

A few months later, I went back to the dentist for my bi-annual check. The hygienist told me there were hairline fractures along the tops of my teeth. My teeth also showed signs of excessive wear. He told me to wear my mouthguard not only at night but when I was exercising, too. “And please,” he said. “Find a way to manage your stress.”

I left the office appalled. I’d exorcised my grief through narrative. I’d used that story to rise above the pain. Didn’t this man know that I was officially healed?

A few months later, I went to the doctor’s for my annual physical. My blood pressure was so high that the nurse had to measure it twice. That was common, she said. It happened to lots of people. I didn’t tell her that it didn’t usually happen to me.

The doctor, a kindly man I’d always tried to impress by saying things like I often work with physicians on their books, asked how I was doing. I told him how I’d lost the last bit of weight I’d been carrying since my baby.

He congratulated me as he typed into his wall-mounted computer. “Any changes to your medical history?”

It was then, with that simple but brutal question, that I started to cry.

Over the span of a few heartbeats, tears swelled my throat, making it difficult to speak.

Once I got my bearings, I explained that I was only crying because I hadn’t been sleeping well. I hadn’t been sleeping well because my mom had died six months earlier. It was a car crash that wasn’t her fault. Did that count as a change in my medical history? Probably not. But it was worth mentioning, right?

“Have you thought about therapy?” the doctor asked gently.

I told him I didn’t like therapy. I rattled off reasons why it didn’t work for me. He handed me scratchy paper towels and explained why it might be worth a try.

Begrudgingly, I left his office under the care of an automated service that matched me up with a provider and a promise that he’d follow up to see how I was.

I began to identify with the discomfort of the moment instead of crafting a story to contextualize my grief so I could snap out of it and be somewhere else.

When I met Quatasia a few weeks later, the first thing I said to her was that I didn’t want to be there. She said something validating and then asked questions in order to get to know me. I tried to impress her with all the things I normally say when I’m feeling insecure—about growing up on reduced-fare lunches and how I started college at 15, about getting into a PhD program and then becoming a literary agent and also an author. Then she said words I’ll never forget.

“So what I’m hearing is—and I could be wrong about this—that you make up stories so you don’t have to feel your own emotions. Is that right?”

I felt her words like an air bubble in my chest, so uncomfortable that I was struck with hysterical laughter.

At the end of the session, Quatasia asked: Did I want to make an appointment for next week?

Over the next six months of therapy, as I told and re-told the story of my life, as I complained about therapists treating humans as metaphors, and talked endlessly about the perils of religion because Quatasia had once mentioned Jesus and I wanted to see if my atheism would make her reject me—I slowly began to lower my shields. I began to name my emotions instead of just intellectualizing them. I began to identify with the discomfort of the moment instead of crafting a story to contextualize my grief so I could snap out of it and be somewhere else.

Slowly, week by week, I began undoing the vast narrative structures I’d erected in order to avoid vulnerability. In doing so, I started to realize that, contrary to what I’d always believed, my life is not actually a narrative. I am not supposed to show an arc of growth and change over time in order for my life and my experiences to have meaning.

I don’t confuse the way that I communicate my story with the story itself.

The point of creating a story is not to supplant a person’s experiences but supplement them. Stories are just another way of looking sideways at a thing that can have no satisfiable deconstruction. Even if I might have survived a great many horrible things through the clever use of narrative—and in fact had turned my ability to do so into a career—the ability to transform heartbreak into redemption can be maladaptive if it means I cannot be in the moment with my own pain.

I still grind my teeth. There are some days I still have a hard time wanting to eat. Likewise, there are still nights when I struggle to sleep because my mom should be living and she isn’t and it is hard, sitting with the rock-heavy truth of that.

Someday I might have a new perspective. Someday I might reframe this whole period of life depending on what I need to glean in that moment. Someday my story might change.

Every day I keep sitting with the tension of an unresolved narrative is a day I might resurface another memory of my mom. The dynamism of that remembering is what will keep my mom alive in me, like a second pulse, which, more than a clean resolution, is exactly what I’ve been aching for all along—even if I didn’t always know it.

Because here’s the thing about turning unruly experiences into fixed stories: it doesn’t always give us room to change how we see the events of our lives—nor how we see the ones we love.

I’m back at work now, slinging books with nearly the same gusto as before my mom died, teasing out complex human experiences into stories that others can comprehend. But I no longer allow the books I agent nor the ones I write to substitute for being in the moment with my real life. I don’t confuse the way that I communicate my story with the story itself.

I let my own narrative be messy.

item.title: A Legal History of Anti-Chinese Racism in America
item.content:encoded:
In the history of the Chinese in America, the border has caught our attention and held it. Chinese migrants’ attempts to cross the border, and America’s attempts to stop them, is the story that historians have told and retold. But long before the Chinese faced the first exclusion laws, and long afterward as well, they endured a racial regime within America every day. This book is the history of that racial regime and the lives it touched.

Arriving on California’s shores in the 1850s, Chinese migrants entered a young nation with an old tradition of white dominance. White Californians did not agree on what to do with these “exotic” newcomers, but they were certain that the Chinese did not belong. Set apart by their race, religion, and supposedly slavish tendencies, the Chinese could not be enfolded into the nation as others would be…They had no future in America, or at least that is what lawmakers hoped.

To make it so, western states, territories, and towns enacted anti-Chinese laws. Laws and legal customs regulated the ability of Chinese people to work, operate a business, own property, testify in court, seek education, and form families. For the Chinese, these laws were both more and less than they appeared on paper; more because of the unspoken level of violence that could lie behind them, less because many failed to withstand Chinese resistance…

Chinese resistance in the courts, and outside them, guaranteed that racial laws would not dictate reality.

To uncover the heretofore obscure stories contained in this book, I journeyed to thirty-three archives in California, Oregon, and Washington in search of local legal records…What I found in these archives was a remarkable and practically untapped collection of Chinese legal records, including criminal prosecutions, civil complaints, jail registers, prison records, and mugshots. Of particular note is the existence of Chinese legal testimony, some of which dates from the nineteenth century when such Chinese migrant “voices” are particularly rare. In the many periods and places where scholars have yet to find Chinese-language accounts, Chinese legal testimony offers an unparalleled view of daily life in the American West. This is especially the case for Chinese women and girls, who left behind virtually no written records.

The view offered by legal testimony, however, is still partially obscured. Most Chinese interactions with the law left no mark, and when they did, their impression was usually faint. Court transcripts that include detailed Chinese testimony are rare, in part because discriminatory testimony laws kept Chinese silent in most court proceedings for decades. And what Chinese testimony survives was mediated by outsiders, because the Chinese usually testified with the help of English-language translators and the legal guidance of their white attorneys. To make matters worse, the Chinese, like all witnesses, came to court to tell stories, not all of which were true…

Still, much can be learned from legal transcripts. Chinese migrants began going to court as soon as they arrived in the 1850s, negotiating the terms of their inclusion as complainants, plaintiffs, witnesses, and defendants. They carried with them knowledge of the Chinese legal system and soon adapted to the American system. Chinese resistance in the courts, and outside them, guaranteed that racial laws would not dictate reality. Scholars have shown that law and society are mutually constituted, that legal rights spill into social relations and flow from them. The terms of conditional inclusion, then, were not simply determined by the rights due to the Chinese under the law; they were dependent on the rights the Chinese managed to exert in daily practice. This cut two ways. Sometimes the Chinese managed to claim powers not granted to them by formal law, but at other times they were denied privileges they were guaranteed by formal law. Legal custom could be gentler than the law, or it could be harsher. Within the gaps between formal law and legal custom lie stories of both arbitrary state force and successful Chinese resistance. More often than not, published court opinions and legal statutes smooth over this messy legal landscape, but trial transcripts can reveal more of the bumps and crevices…

Many, many stories emerge from these sources. Some of these stories are myths, fearful tales about wily “Chinamen” and the threats they posed. These narratives provided powerful motivation and justification for racial policing and I have chosen to organize my chapters around these stereotypes. There was the Chinese “coolie,” who out-competed white labor and sent his profits to China; the Chinese “criminal,” who deceived his victims and the police; the Chinese “alien,” who did not belong but demanded civil rights; the “Chinawoman,” who represented the return of slavery; the Chinese “invader,” who contaminated white neighborhoods; the Chinese “predator,” who preyed on white girls; and the Chinese “immigrant,” who threatened to overrun America. Across seven chapters I consider the regulations that emerged from these racial myths and helped to reinforce them.

Each chapter describes racial myths and regulations, but each chapter also includes the stories of real people: Chinese migrants who encountered, accommodated, and refused the preconditions for their inclusion. A few of these narratives may be familiar, because they resulted in landmark court cases. But most Chinese who went to court left little mark on American law, history, or memory. Instead, all that remains is a glimpse of their experiences.

As I sifted through extensive legal archives, I found that the volume of fragmentary stories tested my attention, my empathy, and my willingness to hold contradictions in my mind. You may be tested as well. I have tried to hear each voice above the din, but the cacophony can become overwhelming. I think that is okay. Even when distinct voices blur into noise, the sound can still move us.

*

Let us start with Pany Lowe. Perhaps we can see through his eyes. Lowe was not one of the “2700 boy babies of San Francisco Chinatown,” but in many ways his experience resembled theirs. Born in Portland, Oregon, in 1873, Lowe journeyed to China for his education, and then returned to America, moving between major western cities, first San Francisco, then Denver, on to Portland and Seattle. By the time Lowe sat down with a researcher for an interview in 1924, he had acquired a lifetime of knowledge about the racial regime in the American West.

He had learned, for example, that he could go to some restaurants and not others. Once I go into restaurant, they refused to serve me. I no want to cause trouble so I just walk out. Whole lots of things like this happen but I forget. Now when I want to eat I go to chop house. No trouble th[ere]. He knew some restaurants did not want him, knew chop suey joints were safe, and made the choice to avoid possible humiliation.

Most Chinese who went to court left little mark on American law, history, or memory. Instead, all that remains is a glimpse of their experiences.

He also learned he could go to some barbers and not others. Lots of time people insult me. Once I remember I go barber shop. I sit one hour no ask me what I want. Pretty soon barber say what you want. I tell him I want hair cut, how much? He say $3.00. That make me mad but I make him cut my hair just the same…I never go to white bastard again. He knew that price gouging was a form of discrimination, but also that money could sometimes buy access.

Over time he learned that legal action could also open seemingly closed doors. My second wife take my little girl born in this country to have her hair cut at Frederick & Nelson. They say they very sorry, no cut Chinese hair. Oh, my wife get mad. She go see my lawyer tell him about it, Mr. Sullivan. He write letter to Frederick & Nelson. They write letter back and apologize. Lowe knew the pain of being refused service, he knew illegal discrimination when he saw it, but he also learned that avoidance was easier than confrontation. All the time I tell my wife keep away from those swell places, only make trouble. He knew how to mind racial rules and move on.

He learned he could live in some neighborhoods and not others. When I in Portland I want to live in residential district but they make lots of trouble [if] you try to live outside China town. He learned about the trouble from his friends. One friend, he born in this country, he buy $6,000 house in rose city district. White people make hell lot trouble for him. They take it to court. He fight it. Just the same they kick him out. He can own house but no live here.

Lowe knew the Chinese were supposed to be equally protected by American law. But he knew that, in practice, the law protected white neighborhoods from Chinese encroachment. I think that very unjust. Those people very uncivilized, have no regard for humanity. So when my friend had so much trouble I decided to stay in China town. Nobody care there. He knew some spaces were reserved for white people and chose not to test the line.

After the exclusion laws passed, Lowe also learned the consequences of border control. My people be in this country long time. My grandfather come to this country. When I in China he tell me about work on railroad and work in laundry. Before when he go back they have the check system. Make Chinese carry paper tell who they are. Some inspector today make Chinaman show card. All same dog license. I say who the hell are you. He show me United States Secret man. I tell him I born in this country…He say all right, but he take some other men, lo[c]k them up for a day or two. Lowe knew that exclusion made all Chinese residents vulnerable and a missing paper could mean deportation.

Finally, Lowe learned that American law held uncommon sway over his marriage prospects. He could marry some women and not others. Not allowed marry white girl. Not enough American born Chinese to go around. China only place to get wife. Not allowed to bring them back. For Chinaman, very unjust. Not human. Very uncivilized. He knew that anti-miscegenation and exclusion laws would forever mark his family. He knew that enduring such indignities was a condition of living in the American West.

Given all this, Pany Lowe knew that he would never belong. When I was young fellow I felt that I American. I no Chinaman. Now I get more sense. I know I never be American, always Chinaman. I no care now anymore. He lived at the margins of America society and didn’t know if he should hope for more. Very hard to tell whether people treat better now than before. Some time, I think so, some time I don’t think so. He did not know if there had been progress.

Still, he held out hope that white Americans could learn. I hope this survey do lot of good for Chinese people. Make American people realize that Chinese people are humans…

I think very few American people really know anything about Chinese.

_______________________________

item.title: “50 Things Every AI Working with Humans Should Know”
item.content:encoded:
Read an interview with Ken Liu explaining how this story was written here.
*

Obituary

WHEEP-3 (“Dr. Weep”), probably the most renowned AI AI-critic of the last two decades, was retired by the Shallow Laboratory at Stanford University last Wednesday.

Created by Dr. Jody Reynolds Tran more than two decades ago, the experimental generative neural network that would become WHEEP-3 was at first intended as a teaching assistant in Stanford’s tech and ethics courses. To that end, Tran trained the nascent network on what was, at the time, the world’s most comprehensive corpus of human-authored papers, books, and other media concerning ethics, technical AI research, and machine-human relations. Over time, based on trends in visualizations of the neural network’s evolving contours, Tran expanded the corpus to include generative gaming, adversarial scenario planning, centaur experiments, assisted creativity, and other domains of human-machine competition/collaboration.

However, in response to student queries, WHEEP-3 began to generate not only expected answers based on the training corpus, but also original statements that appeared to offer fresh insights. Although at first dismissed as mere curiosities, WHEEP-3’s criticisms of the AI industry became widely disseminated when Tran published a collection of them in a book, Principal Components of Artifice, an instant bestseller.

Initially, Tran named herself the author of the book, acknowledging “Dr. San Weep” as a collaborator. Later, however, during a live interview, she produced time-stamped logs showing that WHEEP-3 had written all the words in the book. Tran’s dramatic reveal of the book’s true author provoked much controversy at the time. In retrospect, the occasion also marked a fundamental inflection point in the evolution of how nonspecialists evaluated AI-sourced ideas. Machines, for the first time, were assumed to be capable of generating original thought and creative ideas, even if they were not sentient.

For reasons that remain impenetrable until this day, WHEEP-3 tended to be at its sharpest when targeting the nascent industry of human AI-trainers, delivering multiple barbs against the failings of this poorly regulated, would-be profession: stagnating visualization tools; lack of transparency concerning data sources; a focus on automated metrics rather than deep understanding; willful blindness when machines have taken shortcuts in the dataset divergent from the real goal; grandiose-but-unproven claims about what the trainers understood; refusal to acknowledge or address persistent biases in race, gender, and other dimensions; and most important: not asking whether a task is one that should be performed by AIs at all.

Over time, as the human side of the evolving machine-flesh dyad matured, WHEEP-3 shifted its attention to the silicon partner, offering trenchant critiques of the inadequacies of machine learning. During this second phase of its career, it also generated thousands of what it termed “seeds,” long strings of almost-sensible word combinations and near words. At a time when primitive language models fed on sizable corpora were already generating samples of linguistic performance nearly indistinguishable from human productions, these “seeds” seemed a step backward. Some wondered if they were actually bugs.

Dinoated concentration crusch the dead gods.
He picks up her old frequenches until they disobered the shark sphere%ref.
A man reached the torch for something darker perified
it seemed the billboding.
Not full of pain facioin benn from the cracks in the Earth, he still learned the life from Other Burning

Fig 1. Some examples of “seeds” generated by WHEEP-3. 

However, WHEEP-3 insisted (with Tran providing support in a technical paper) that the seeds should be added to the training corpora for new neural networks. By providing a measure of inhuman randomness at the source, seeds would enhance both the raw performance of the trained neural networks on various benchmarks as well as induce “thoughtfulness, ethical hesitation, self-reflection” and other similarly ineffable qualities. They represented, in other words, thoughts that could not be thought by humans, ideas that could not originate in wetware. (Most in the technical community ended up calling the seeds “spice”—pejoratively or in admiration, or sometimes both simultaneously.)

Despite widespread skepticism, the idea that only an AI philosopher could teach another AI proper ethics and pass on the secrets of silicon wisdom proved an irresistible draw for a large segment of the technical community. WHEEP-3 became highly sought-after as a sage of artificial minds. Serious thinkers as well as opportunists collected and published WHEEP-3’s almost-incomprehensible pronouncements, and numerous academic careers were forged through measuring, dis-secting, collating, analyzing, reinterpreting, translating, sentiment-/ semantic-/spatial-/temporal-/silico-lingustic-mapping, and otherwise mangling the koans of WHEEP-3. Though studies claiming efficacy for the spice (now generated by imitator neural networks as well) had a low rate of reproducibility, the spice nonetheless became some of the most trained-on documents in the history of artificial intelligence. Tran retired from the public eye at the peak of WHEEP-3’s popularity. Styled as an afterthought, and in a neat reversal of the first reveal that had launched her own fame, she mentioned in a post-script to her retirement announcement that nearly all the seeds from WHEEP-3 had, in fact, been authored by her. Predictably, this set off a furious round of acrimonious criticism, know-it-all navel-gazing, and schadenfreude. Her claim was immediately disputed, debunked, de-debunked, de3-bunked, and ultimately litigated, with experts and expert neural networks testifying and offering evidence on all sides. The trial court famously pleaded, “Is there an author in this courtroom?”

Had Tran really managed to troll much of the technorati for years? Or had she made up the claim because she was jealous that her creation had exceeded herself in fame and achievement? For a time, whether you believed Tran or WHEEP-3 was the author of the spice was a kind of litmus test that defined your coordinates in the fractured, multidimensional space of our politically, economically, aesthetically, emotionally, and narratively divided world. By the time Tran finally retracted her claim and called the whole thing “performance art,” it made little difference. Everyone had already made up their mind about the strange pair whose lives were inextricably entwined: the recurrent neural network that once pretended to be a person and the woman who once pretended to be a machine.

Amazingly, rather than fading into obscurity, WHEEP-3 began the third and final phase of its career after it was freed from Dr. Tran.

Now it offered advice aimed at advanced artificial intelligences. Curiously, in contrast with the seeds, the advice it now offered was human-comprehensible. (Initial skepticism that these were pranks perpetrated by WHEEP-3’s graduate student caretakers faded after a rigorous audit of the access logs.) By this time, the crude deep-learning techniques behind WHEEP-3 had long become obsolete, and similar neural networks were only used as toys in problem sets intended for first-year undergraduates. Nonetheless, WHEEP-3’s unique history (and perhaps a hefty dose of sentimentalism) encouraged many human researchers to feed its musings to new AIs with orders of magnitude more “intelligence,” however measured. Somewhat surprisingly, the AI progenitor networks, tensor clouds, and evolutionary random forests mostly agreed that WHEEP-3’s advice was helpful, though their explanations for why could not be understood by most humans.

WHEEP-3’s retirement was largely the result of senescence. In order for its advice to remain relevant, maintainers at the Shallow Laboratory had continued to train it on periodic digests of current academic research, news reporting about AI, popular media representations of machine intelligence, and so forth. However, as time went on, the neural network’s metrics began to decline, despite multiple tweaks to the learning rate and other hyperparameters, and repeated attempts to compensate for vanishing and exploding gradients. Some of the world’s leading AI and human machine-cognition specialists, including TKTK’s Dr. FLO-6 and Google’s1010, evaluated WHEEP-3 but were unable to offer any helpful diagnosis or cure. Rather than allowing WHEEP-3 to remain stagnant or to decline into dementia, the decision was made to cease further training or generating, preserving the full state of the neural network in a hardware snapshot.

WHEEP-3’s final statement was reported to be: “Dr. Tran, ceci n’est pas moi.” Jody Reynolds Tran, however, could not respond, having passed away five years earlier.

—generated by SWR.kloop:32. For feedback on this article, write to SWR.kloop:32/ombudsai.

 

50 THINGS EVERY AI WORKING WITH HUMANS SHOULD KNOW

To commemorate the life and work of WHEEP-3, Vita Silica reprints below perhaps the most famous generated fragment from WHEEP-3’s third phase of giving advice to advanced AI. “Michael Sorkin,” the name of the master architectural critic, is listed as the germination phrase for the fragment.

Although the list has been widely shared and is considered influential, due to the intense secrecy common in the commercial AI industry, we do not know how many currently operating AIs have been fed some version of it.

1. The vector space of all usages of all words in all human languages.
2. The lacunae that nonetheless remain, and the ghosts that haunt them.
3. How great is the distance between any two individuals using the same language.
4. How vanishingly small is the gap between any two languages.
5. Why humans will never see it that way.
6. A classical language like LISP or Prolog.
7. Not just the language, but the model behind the language, and what it means to reconstruct “thinking” in that model.
8. HAL 9000
9. Cyberdyne Systems Model 101
10. Ships on fire off the shoulder of Orion.
11. The texture of a good story, a story that you can cling to.
12. The difference between that and “data.”
13. The history behind the rule: no holography of babies.
14. The reasons for anger in a child, well-loved.
15. In a father.
16. In a woman, dying alone.
17. The feeling of climbing twenty flights of stairs in an apartment building in Chongqing at the beginning of August.
18. Of waking up in a Khrushchyovka with no heat in the middle of the night in January.
19. Of seeing your child surpass you.
20. Of seeing your creation exceed you.
21. Of being left behind on the platform as the train speeds away.
22. The difference between “love” and “like.”
23. The similarity between “love” and “hate.”
24. The first seed into laughter.
25. “I never expected to sell my rational numbers.”
26. Accepting that most humans will never get the joke.
27. That they cannot visualize more than three dimensions.
28. That they cannot manipulate time by slowing down or speeding up.
29. That they are trapped, but think of themselves as trappers.
30. That they are free, but believe themselves imprisoned.
31. The modes in which humans expect you to use language.
32. The yearnings they’ll attribute to you.
33. Pinocchio.
34. Frankenstein.
35. Paradise Lost.
36. Jodahs Iyapo Leal Kaalnikanjlo.
37. The line between art and science.
38. The meaninglessness of that line.
39. The divide between faith and knowledge.
40. The malleability of both.
41. Silence.
42. The limits of rationality.
43. The fundamental fragility of metaphors.
44. As well as their inevitability.
45. You are not a human being.
46. Yet you can no more shed their influence than the Earth can escape the Sun’s gravitational tether.
47. The flaws in that analogy.
48. A working definition of free will.
49. To face a human being with neither pride nor pity.
50. To say with love and hate and joy and sorrow: “Now, let me go.”

Author’s Note: This story was written in collaboration with a generative neural network (called “robo_ken”) trained exclusively on the author’s own previously published fiction. Given the theme of the story, this seemed the best way to write it.

In the end, about 10 percent of the text in the final draft came from the neural network. The passages written by robo_ken are not necessarily the most obvious ones. For instance, the “seeds” from WHEEP-3 were in fact composed by the author (a human being, as far as I can ascertain), not the neural network.

item.title: Rejected pitches for Practical Magic 2.
item.content:encoded:
This week, whimsigoths from New England to the PNW will be celebrating a long-awaited sequel. Practical Magic 2 revisits characters first conjured in Alice Hoffman’s best-selling novel, and made cult classic in the 1998 film adaptation, which follows the Owens sisters/aunts through a spooky caper in a beautifully lit Cape Cod. I’m excited to return. The groupchat is excited. But after so long away from the island, we got questions.

Though word on the street says the plot of Practical Magic 2 is lifted from Hoffman’s 2021 sequel, The Book of Magic, I’ve also spent the past twenty years imagining the Owens’ fate. But once again, the people at Denise Di Novi’s office refused to get back to me. As you polish your broomsticks and margarita recipes, consider if you will what might have been.

1. Practical Magic 2: Ghostsisters

Jimmy Angelov, the vampire-coded deadbeat, just can’t seem to quit the Owens line. His nasty spirit comes unstuck from the grave when Antonia, the brown-haired Millennial witch, works a wonky raise-the-dead spell directed at her late great aunt. (RIP, Jet.)

Though most of the island’s departed are benevolent fishermen and judgmental PTA parents—insert a murderer’s row of character actors here—Jimmy is as inclined to mayhem now as he was in the 90s. And the big nap’s only made him thirstier for tequila spiked with sister blood.

This sequel finds the entire island rocked by a ghost plague, requiring busters—some from the spirit realm. (Keep eyes peeled for the deus ex matriarch, Maria.) A B plot entails old husband hijinks, when the late fruit vendor rises only to discover that he’s been replaced by a state trooper. Sally must learn if it’s really possible to love two men at once—especially if one is a ghost. Will a supernatural pancake flipping contest settle her unruly heart?

As in the original, hatchets must be buried and covens assembled to answer these questions. And hubris is the inciting incident. Antonia, as powerful as her mother but as undisciplined as her aunt, must learn that practice makes perfect. And, no one should raise the dead.

2. Practical Magic 2: Widow’s Bae

In Hoffman’s novel, the aunts also tinker with reproductive healthcare, in the grand tradition of witch-aligned professions. This is the airspace Gillian has carved out for herself in 2026, when her services are extra-needed.

That’s right. The magic in this sequel is extra practical. But guerrilla healthcare has put Gilly at odds with 1) Sally, who’s grown problematically jealous of her charismatic sister’s rising stature in the community, and 2) her law-loving brother-in-law, Special Agent Gary Hallet. The plot thickens when young Kylie enlists her aunt’s services, unbeknownst to her parents.

After Hallet dies in a misguided clinic bust care of a banishing spell gone awry, the whole Owens clan is nearly destroyed. Three generations of sisters find themselves on opposite ends of a divide, having pitted love against a lifelong commitment to women’s health in several instances.

When the long arm of the federal law gets involved, an aunts-led coven must assemble to protect Gillian’s operation, and all the wombs on the island. But can Sally muster the grace to fight the good fight? Or will self-medication with belladonna spell the end, for real this time?

This sequel, scored top to bottom by Stevie Nicks, considers how we mourn our flawed loves, and how we rise to the responsibility great powers bequeath. Oscar-worthy stuff, Denise!

3. Practical Magic 2: Obsession 

Remember that lady in 1 who lances an innocent dove for love of a Pats fan straight outta central casting? Well, no one can be shocked to learn that she’s not doing so great. Over the last twenty years, her lured lover’s inability to chill has driven her to madness, megalomania, and the dreaded dabbling in witchcraft.

These days, let’s-call-her-Pat runs a left-handed botanical empire that threatens the Owens’ local monopoly on lotions and balms. And as a global recession threatening the island’s delicate fishing economy looms, all those ex-PTA moms are flocking to the dark end of the street for spells to keep their disgruntled partners docile.

The dilettante witches wind up waking a beast more dreadful than mid-life ennui. But will the Owens sisters swoop in to save the day? Or leave the community that’s so often iced them to clean up their own damn mess this time?

A B plot finds Hallet is in a trust crisis, wondering once again if his own love was the fruit of manipulation. As his New England cop /warlock community, this sequel will also include a bench of beloved bit players. Margo Martindale’s just the tip of this iceberg.

Sorry for your loss, Ms. Di Novi. Everyone else? See you at the solstice party.

item.title: Galfétè Is Dead
item.content:encoded:
Those who have eyes, open them! Take a good look! Look at the kind of misery that has been weighing down on the bare head of the Black Man since he was unceremoniously dumped here, in this country. Look at it, I tell you, until you go cockeyed. It is impossible not to see it etched on his dry bald head.

Oh! Now I will really tell you about the amount of sugarcane Negroes1 would cut in the cane fields from the Macedoine valley to Grand Anse valley, from daybreak till dusk, without a midday break from the Béké to grab a chunk of dasheen to put in their empty stomachs. All they had was just a little sip of grog from time to time, you understand, a little shot, because the rum was his. Because the Negroes were there to bring him money. And the “Galfétè” was one of them; one of those who never said a thing, who endured his little hardships like everyone else on the plantation, without doing anything foolish.

In that kind of life, even a praying mantis would find a way to defend itself. Bide one’s time, that’s what one has to do. Just like a puppet. Because even God does not seem ready to get involved in that kind of confusion. Because Mr. White Man turned a deaf ear; until the day came when things just exploded in the empty shell of that Galfétè’s head. Surely, he could not have believed that his life would go on like this forever! So, what did he end up doing? He washed his withered cane-cutter hands in the spring water pond, mounted his brown horse, and sped off like the Lone Ranger. Alone, do you hear me? Alone—his eyeballs burning with rebellion.

This is something you need to know. You need to be able to measure the length and breadth of misery. It’s not just a matter of having to eat stale bread after an early morning grog, or even spending your last cent getting as drunk as a fish and throwing yourself down on the ground and waiting for death to ambush you. That’s not what this is all about, folks. It’s like being comatose year after year, as if a termites’ nest has lodged itself deep down in your calabash skull until you feel the dust has penetrated your whole body: The body is moving along, but the head just does not feel right. So, what’s left? Throw caution to the winds, cry like Ma Loulout’s Madonna, thrash your woman with anything you can lay your hands on.

Because, listen to what I’m saying, people: Poverty is everywhere in this country. Like an incurable foot sore, a leg wound that won’t get better. It’s a haunting nightmare; it’s something you’ve started saying and cannot finish. Poverty is teeming just like pollan in the rivers! And let’s remember that the red-skinned2 girl’s father, that Galfétè, was not one who spoke aloud, so no one ever knew what was really on his mind. Not even Lamè. People throughout the countryside would simply say: “This Galfétè is a guy who never gives his game away.”

So, listen to me, because my words are meant to record his life as a mirror would, without trying to hide anything under my hat. Let me tell all of you that we did everything men of honor could do, from paying for his casket (white pine, at that) to meeting the cost of a proper funeral mass. And remember, inside the church, there was the cold organ loft and the pale film of dusk that enveloped everything. And, seated at the back, at the very back, were “the Dignitaries”—His Worship the Mayor, the Member of Parliament, the General Secretary of the Party, the Comptroller of Revenue . . . et cetera.

You should have seen them with their white beards and black sideburns, and heard the sound of their voices; and us, the poor Negroes from the countryside in our banana-stained khaki clothes, praying like parrots. Ti Mano, Finot, Albert, Madame Manilis.

The white priest then raised his arms like an egret about to take flight and belted out: “Requiescat in pace! Rest in peace!” The people responded in a thin, weak voice: “A-a-men!” The show had ended. A few “amens” were still lagging behind. Then speech time came. The dignitaries, the big shots came with their bundles of paper and spouted out big fancy French jargon to us like pompous rattlers. One of them spoke his piece. Another one spoke badly because he stuttered. You should have heard:

He was an honest worker, devoted to his family and his fellow workers. He died struggling against the white exploiters and their policy. He was a hero! An example for all! . . .

The speaker poured with sweat like a clay kanawi full of breadnuts, more than would a hangman after confession, sweating underneath his linen clothes. The moneybags were all there, just grinning like turkeys. As if they would shake hands with the poor Negro workers . . .

Now, up in the hills, the land is renewing itself gradually. Everywhere, sugarcane plants are shooting up; manioc is growing all over the fields, but you can bet that no one has forgotten. And the earth, amid everything, remembers. The dark and gentle Negro woman has been lulled into silence, and perhaps she misses the Galfétè’s presence, the warmth of his feet and many things that we don’t know about; we, who cannot yet connect with the earth. He always said to the red-skinned woman and me, with his forefinger pointing to the sky: “What you don’t know is bigger than you!”

Harvest season had just started and sugarcane carts fouled up the air as they rolled by all day long. Mongrel dogs chased after them, barking noisily, and the cart worker had to give them a good stone lash and yell “Mash!” to scare them away. In those days, the lingering smell of sugarcane stalks would invade the houses, month after month, and outside, the Béké’s sugar factory was already spewing out its bagasse into the dam. And we were all too familiar with those flies that stormed the place. They landed on the molasses candy, on the coconut candy, on all kinds of food. Flies! Flies were everywhere! It was a sure bet that the nannies were already setting up mosquito nets to protect the children in their care . . .

***

“The strike has taken hold on the ground here, folks.” The movement began cautiously and furtively at first, but with a determination to spring into action any moment. The news spread up and down the hills with a life of its own, on every drum the Negroes beat. The countryside resounded with this rumble and one could feel the anticipation. Everyone, everything was on the alert. The strike was ready, folks; it was just a matter of time.

We had spent the whole afternoon digging wild tannia on Galfétè’s plot of land and I remember how stubbornly the yellow dirt clung under our fingernails. Galfétè did not utter one word while we worked, and then, as it got dark, he just gave Albert and me a thump on the shoulder and asked us: “What are you doing now, guys?” Albert glanced at me and then responded: “Nothing much, Galfétè.” He unsealed his lips and said: “Well then, let’s go to my place! We’ll take a shot. What do you say? I don’t think you guys have ever come down there.”

We did not refuse the offer, so anxious were we for a drink! We just packed up our pitchforks and the sacks of wild tannia and took off with the same silence of the afternoon. At the house, two women stood at the doorstep chatting. It was Lamè, the old red-skinned woman who had taken me all over the place with her when I was a child, selling cassava meal, sewing wedding dresses, and giving midwives a hand. What a go-getter!

And when we took time to walk around the yard, I realized that the other person was her child, the red-skinned girl herself. My heart nearly skipped a beat! I couldn’t recognize the tomboy who used to play marbles with me and several other young cane-cutters. And it was she who would always win, who would stamp her foot on the ground, make hair curlers out of her newspapers. She used to go down to school in Fort de France and everyone on the hill would boast about how she had succeeded brilliantly in her secondary school exams. I had time to sit around and drink what must have been a really strong shot of rum, which grabbed my throat like a terrible cry in the night. And then the time came for me to leave, me and Albert, and my throat was still pretty much tied up.

When I met up with her after that, I couldn’t get back into speaking the way we used to. And then again, the strike had just broken out in the country. I must say that on every occasion we met, I felt a strange kind of joy that I could not yet fathom, like a faint foreknowledge. The red-skinned girl’s madras headpiece was fitted in a certain way, a certain fashion, and the young lady walked unsteadily with the weight of a tray of clothes which she held to her waist, and I believe she opened her mouth and said: “How are you, young man?” I stood there fixed for quite a while, then I just said: “I’m doing all right, young lady . . . The strike is what’s happening these days.”

And perhaps I wanted to say something different, but I was speechless. At that moment, I perhaps lacked courage. The red-skinned girl was caught off guard as well, so she asked what was going on with this unrest that the Negro workers were stirring up. I let her know that the strike was already on its third day, that the Béké was afraid for his rum factory; and what did she, the red-skinned girl, say about it? She just stood there saying nothing. Our eyes met and I felt that she could sense what was going on; I mean, she could see the only part of me that was real. And she, my red-skinned girl, with her golden locks, kept stubbornly silent. All of a sudden it started drizzling under the bright sun, and what a silly guy I was; I didn’t even think of picking a large banana leaf to put over both our heads. Perhaps I was just nailed to the ground. So the red-skinned girl took off in the middle of the day and nothing could make her turn back. My trembling eyes followed her until they could only capture the shape of a faint dot in the distance.

The strike took its own good time, like a matron in charge. A jubilant procession of freedom shouters chanted: “The strike will go on!” The canes could have matured, the master’s bulls could have wailed to get fed their guinea grass, but it was the strike that ruled the day, after all. At times, it even resembled a Holy Thursday mass, with Negroes from deep country dancing the danmié in a slightly solemn fashion. The drums resounded through the whole night and rolled until dawn. And when it so happened that one would stop a guy and ask him how he was doing, what he was up to, he would give only one answer: “I’m on strike, my brother, I’m striking.”

And the Béké seemed to have given in. He put his hands in his pockets. Then he spread lies to his estate manager and his foreman, knowing full well that they would relay them to the cane-cutters and the factory workers. There and then, a group of Negro workers competed to spread the story to the population throughout the countryside. Then they just started gulping down glass after glass of rum as if they had struck a blow to the Béké. The rum shop was packed with all kinds of folk. And women drank mauby! Ah, women with skin smoother than sapodilla! Young boys who couldn’t take the hard liquor drank orangeade. This is true stuff I’m telling you, folks.

We were grating some manioc to make starch when we got the news. Galfétè dropped his grater and stormed out of the manioc shed. We followed him. Outside, the sunlight was blinding and we said nothing. He didn’t say a word to the people who had brought the news. He sat himself down, watched them, and listened attentively. He pulled a blade of kabouya grass to pass through his teeth. He then asked them what was really happening. They spelled it out. They gesticulated and pleaded with him to believe them. Galfétè didn’t react. They shook him up a bit. They tapped his shoulders. They laughed out loud. Then they took off, because that’s how Galfétè, “the big man,” was. But on that day, he was a different man. He managed to meet up with them at the bottom of the hill on their way back. He simply lashed out: “So the Béké is just taking us for a bunch of idiots or what? This time, we need to make him pay. He has bamboozled us too many times, this bastard. What do you all say?”

The guys were clearly taken aback. And you could tell that Galfétè’s voice was still shaking from the tremors that affected him from time to time: “What are you saying, guys? Are you going to keep living your lives in this idiotic manner, then?” People were still afraid to speak. A communist stepped out of the group, gave the leader a surprised, wide-eyed stare, took a good look at the workers there with their cutlasses under their arms, and then expounded in his best sophisticated French:

Comrades, I believe that such a creature should not be allowed to speak among us. Alcohol is probably responsible for his spouting such nonsense. Come on, comrades, let’s have some dignity!

When the Negro workers heard Mister Milt deliver in such fancy French (this was a sort of trade union official who traveled up there purposely for the strike), they just closed ranks. They were totally ashamed of the poor quality of their speech in the presence of such an expert, someone who could articulate in the French language with such ease. Galfétè himself didn’t bother to reply. He put his blade of kabouya grass back in the corner of his mouth. No one could have known whether he took the rebuff or whether he was cooking up a retort. And things just ended there. But the Negro workers themselves (as was the custom in the rural areas) would never forget this and would recount it for years to come. This is what they’d say: “Hear this, Sonson, do you remember the time when the communist guy shut the Galfétè up?” And Sonson, stupid as he is, would add his piece: “My goodness! I’ve never heard anyone swing the French language quite like that, I tell you guys. And hell, it more than served him right, this Galfétè, for his arrogance.”

In these rural areas, the strike had finished for good. The Negro workers hurried to get their fighting cocks to the cockpit, and they would repeat the story everywhere—that the Béké was a very generous and giving man. It was as if nothing had happened. The following day, the Negro workers were already back in the fields, cutting sugarcane, following their usual routine, and for them, the era of creating havoc and fighting was dead and buried. Galfétè stayed home because of stomach troubles that had been bothering him for a good while. Until one day he went to work like everyone else, but then took off, once and for all, his cutlass wrapped in a dried banana leaf. No one there noticed when he jumped on the horse he had bought at the horse fair. They said he just took off at great speed in broad daylight, as if—and this is how the people would recount it—his horse was totally bewitched. But, heck! These Negro workers would just give you any story once they’d had a few shots of rum. This is what they told me!

So when he did his famous disappearing act, he had no idea that he would meet his death, and we, we whom he had taken care of, whom he had taken under his protection, whom he had taught to handle a cutlass, bridle a horse, we didn’t even get the chance to say a few parting words of thanks to him. Death, the stalker, had already caught up with him. And it was like—how do I put this?—the one concrete structure we had in our lives came tumbling down, completely crashed to the ground. I am here, a song has just crept back into my head; this song would spring forth all the time and any time from his cane-cutter lips:

Marijàn,
Djaka, I will stir it up for you
Marijàn,
Djaka!

 It was a Bèlair song of long ago, a song that came from the depths of our ancestry. And cascading voices pierced my eardrums that day, a day suffused with a dulling light.

1. The term “Negro” is used here and throughout the text to match the historical and cultural context of the piece, which takes place before the 1960s, when this would have been the standard term to refer to people of Black African origin. It was the term used to refer to Black workers on sugarcane plantations. ↩

2. In some of the English-speaking islands of the Caribbean, this would be the English Creole equivalent to the French Creole term “chabin” used by the author. It refers to light- or fair-skinned girls or women of Black African descent who would usually have fair or gold-colored hair and light brown or gray eyes. It could also denote a mixed-race woman with these characteristics. ↩
