item.title: A Maroon Monument
item.content:encoded:
In 1943, amid Word War II, a group of European architects and historians, Siegfried Giedion, Jean Luc Sert, and Ferdinand Léger, summarized their thoughts on monuments in the text “Nine Points on Monumentality.” Writing in a Europe quickly turning to rubble, the authors saw monuments as unique social tools to restore a sense of historicity for a people. On the one hand, monuments were a reminder of a certain sense of wholeness that preceded the ruination around them; on the other hand, monuments translated people’s hopes into powerful and coherent symbols. In their own particular way, monuments helped people survive the war. While the manifesto concluded that “monuments form a link between the past and the future,” hence providing a sense of historical continuity, it also specified that “monuments are only possible in periods in which a unifying consciousness and unifying culture exists.” In this way, “Nine Points on Monumentality” established criteria for the design and understanding of the relationship between monuments and communities. The text’s influence soon extended across the Atlantic, informing the work of architects and urban planners in Latin America during the second half of the twentieth century and beyond.

Nonetheless, when reading the manifesto with contemporary eyes, one cannot avoid the thought that its very premises invite questioning. Particularly the insistence on the adjective “unifying,” attached to notions of culture, consciousness, and historicity, as a requirement for the existence of monuments. Why is “unity” the precondition for monumentality and not its consequence? How would this apply to other modes of consciousness? For example, would a dispersed consciousness of historical continuity produce monuments? What about the schizophrenic consciousness that erupts against linear narratives? And what about a consciousness disturbed by the specters of trauma? Or the consciousness of a radically new way of thinking? A monument to the maroon leader Benkos Biohó, the mythical founder of San Basilio de Palenque, Colombia, offers the opportunity to address some of these questions and to raise new ones.

According to the historical research of Nina de Friedemann and Cristina Navarrete, the creation of numerous palenques, or fortified settlements built by communities of people who had escaped slavery, in Colombian territory coincides with the beginning of the slave trade in Cartagena de Indias. Since the sixteenth century, people who escaped slavery, better known as maroons or “cimarrones,” had headed toward La Matuna, the dense tropical mountain of the Colombian Caribbean. Although the persecution of the maroons by Cartagena’s government was constant and fierce, the jungle terrain of La Matuna and the maroons’ war strategies frustrated the vast majority of military expeditions against them.

One of the most famous of these maroons was Benkos Biohó. According to Navarrete, the name Biojó (Biohó) corresponds to an African king enslaved on the coast of Guinea who organized one of the first palenques in the Colombian coastal savanna. The maroons commanded by the “king of Arcabuco” were feared by their Cartagena neighbors, not only because of their unexpected seizure of roads, but because they represented a real possibility of escape for other enslaved people. In 1603, after Biohó and his maroons foiled repeated attempts by the Crown to subject them to servitude, they were granted a license to circulate through Cartagena and to carry weapons. In 1621, the Crown broke the agreement with the trial and hanging of Biohó.

Though Biohó is remembered in the popular imagination as the founder of San Basilio de Palenque, the historical research of María Cristina Navarrete has polemicized the Palenquero libertarian myth by proposing the existence of two different palenques separated by almost a hundred years. On the one hand, there is Benkos Biohó, who led a fierce palenque in the jungles of La Matuna and who in effect obtained permission to carry a sword and move freely in Cartagena around 1603. On the other hand, there are historical records of the “legal constitution of the town of San Basilio” from the reduction of the rebellious Palenque of San Miguel with the signature of the Entente Cordiale in 1713. Navarrete clarifies that with this contract, the Palenqueros were released from the yoke of slavery and attained territorial self-determination. Needless to say, such recognition came with its caveats, including schooling in Spanish, the establishment of a chapel and accompanying priest, the obligation to carry a passport outside of Palenque at all times, and the population’s incorporation as reserved army for the Spanish Crown.

Benkos Biohó’s monument in San Basilio de Palenque conflates these two histories into one myth: The town was founded in 1603 by Benkos Biohó, also known as the “King of Arcabuco,” after signing the Entente Cordiale in 1713. From then on, a unique culture and language—Palenquero, the only Hispanic creole of the Americas, formed of a blend of Spanish and Kikongo—flourished within its territory. In 1995, San Basilio de Palenque was recognized by UNESCO as “the first free people of the Americas,” giving global resonance to the town’s libertarian myth. With this recognition came the monument to Benkos that concerns us here.

Benkos’s myth comes first to Western eyes through Roberto de Arrázola’s book Palenque: Primer Pueblo Libre de América (1970) and Nina de Friedemann’s Ma Ngombe: guerreros y ganaderos (1989). In fact, de Friedemann was also involved in the creation of the monument with the sculptor Luis Guillermo Vallejo: She brought the bronze to Palenque following UNESCO’s commemoration of the town as part of its program “Routes of Enslaved Peoples: Resistance, Liberty and Heritage” (translated to Spanish as “La ruta del esclavo”).1 Once in Palenque, the sculpture was housed in the town’s little church for almost two years, awaiting its pedestal. During this period previous to its “monumentalization,” the bronze was treated by the people of Palenque as a miraculous image and a kind of saint.2 However, this attitude seemed to change once the sculpture was placed outside the church on a pedestal built by the Palenqueros/as themselves sometime in 1997.

Figure 1. Benkos Biohó’s monument in San Basilio de Palenque, Colombia.

An initial approach to Benkos’s monument as it was then reveals a striking contradiction: The founder, the great maroon leader, is enchained. One hand holds the shackles; the other reaches out, constrained, as the leader looks up and shouts. His body extends upward, but freedom escapes him. Visually, his torso is immobilized by the pedestal: The block of cement pulls him down and keeps him in place. One quick look reveals that the gravitational pull of the diagonal composition comes from the base—and out of it Benkos rises in desperation.3 One can’t help but wonder, where is he rising up from? From what’s visible: the sandy soil of Palenque? Or is he emerging from a symbolic dimension? I propose that the implicit ground from which Benkos tries to escape is none other than the abysmal mouth of the slave ship about to cross the Atlantic. That’s why he is naked and in chains, and that’s why he is reaching upward. Thus, the monument recasts the cimarrón, the self-declared free man, as a captive—and yet the title of the piece is “Benkos rompiendo las cadenas de la esclavitud,” or “Benkos breaking the chains of slavery.” In other words, this monument portrays the maroon warrior as a runaway slave. 

In Vallejo’s sculpture, the representation of freedom depends entirely on the symbolic universe of slavery. Moreover, the monument represents and commemorates Black freedom using the formal elements of the Western canon: orthogonal concentricity, the elevation and interpellation of the gaze of a (static) spectator, and the expressiveness of a heroic gesture. These are a series of plastic choices characteristic of a vision of the monument as a phallic unit of meaning, that is, as upright, impenetrable, and individual. This focus on a single person not only ignores the collective and heterogeneous character of maroon resistance, but also installs an essentialist mode of representation. Ideologically, the monument draws from UNESCO’s whitewashed relationship with slavery, which informs its recognition of Palenque as a Masterpiece of Intangible Heritage. All in all, UNESCO’s commemoration (and the monument) pacifies the political force of maroonage and culturalizes its relentless fight against colonialism, Spanish or otherwise. 

Alongside the anecdotal (what is the story of this man, of this name?), the study of the monument raises questions about the historiographical: how a history is told. In that vein, one might ask: What notion of maroonage does this monument propose? Who is telling this history? How is it told? And in what language? Needless to say, here “language” goes beyond the written word to include visual, material, and spatial elements and configurations. 

The initial installation (probably a temporary platform) showed an important disproportion between the height of the monument’s base (over four meters) and the sculpture’s smaller dimensions. A closer look revealed material differences between the bronze figure and its rudimentary base of concrete and house tiles. For lack of an official plaque, the following denomination was handwritten at the bottom of the pedestal:

Palenke Fundado por BENKOS BIOHO en 16034

As we can see, the syntactic order of the phrase interprets the monument as Palenke’s foundational marker, dating the mythological creation of the settlement by Biohó well before its official recognition by the Spanish Crown in 1713. In this first iteration of the monument, it’s impossible to distinguish Palenke from the figure of its founder: Benkos is Palenke, and Palenke is Benkos. Most importantly, this would be the first and only time the town’s name was written with a “k,” a small but critical point of resistance to Hispanism.

Placed next to the chapel, the monument/foundational stone cast a spell of memorialization over the adjacent area, becoming a landmark of Palenque’s new “historical center.” Slowly but surely, this placement profoundly altered the town’s ancestral built environment by deploying a colonial (Hispanic) spatial arrangement of church-plaza-monument. An ironic, if not confusing, celebration of Palenque’s self-determination as a fierce maroon territory. Why would the descendants of cimarrón warriors resort to the sculptural and spatial syntax of Hispanic colonialism? Were they requesting admission into a specific history?

A few years later, the epigraph was corrected to reference the statue rather than the town. In this second version, the name of the village was also amended, replacing Kikongo’s “ke” ending for its Hispanic transliteration, “que.” The new inscription read:

BENKOS BIOHO fundador de Palenque. 16035

The syntactic reorganization of the new epigraph sought to adjust the coincidence between the town and Benkos Biohó, reinscribing the monument under standardized conventions of historical commemoration. However, the new epigraph maintained the date of the mythical foundation of Palenque, 1603, celebrating the fictional foundation of the settlement. At this point, Benkos’s monument is most paradoxical: The founder and symbol of maroon freedom appears yoked to the pedestal by the chains of slavery (see figures 2 and 3).

Figure 2. The monument with its second epigraph. Photo by Yves Moñino, 2009.

Figure 3. Both inscriptions.

The solution to such an unbearable contradiction was the removal of the chains by the Palenqueros. But then, how to justify the pose and facial expression of the sculpture? Without the chains, the figure was stripped of its symbolic element, and Benkos became a confusing allegory, a mute cry for freedom. Soon after, the epigraph was covered up entirely by a series of steps, leaving in place an homage without a name, a tombstone without a body: a cenotaph (see figure 4).

The community might have left the monument in this state of suspension if not for the government funds that in 2015 sought to institutionalize Benkos’s heroism. Major changes occurred to the monument and its surrounding area in that year. The church’s renovation included the expansion of its square footage and a total makeover of the plaza. Now, a tile design clearly demarcates a path connecting the entrance of the town to the church. The same colored tiles form a heliocentric pattern that extends from the base of the statue toward the church and the plaza, visually marking the monument as the epicenter of Palenque (as shown in figures 5 and 6).

Figure 4. Stairs covering up the pedestal. Photo by Ferrari, 2012.

Figure 5. Progressive urbanization of the plaza in San Basilio de Palenque. Photo by Yves Moñino, 2012 and 2014.

Figure 6. A heliocentric pattern surrounds the base of the monument. Photo by Yves Moñino, 2012 and 2014.

The monument also received a new pedestal and epigraph asserting Benkos’s historical existence and reaffirming his heroism. Printed over a makeshift colonial scroll, the inscription reads:

Benkos Biohó Nació en la segunda mitad del siglo XVI en la region de Biohó una region de la que hacen parte las islas Bijangós en la Guinea Portuguesa (actual Guinea Bissau), en el occidente de África. Benkos Biohó, también conocido como Domingo Biohó, fue un líder que comandó una rebelión de esclavizados cimarrones en el Nuevo Reino de Granada en el siglo XVII. Convirtiéndose en el HÉROE MAYOR del PRIMER PUEBLO LIBRE de américa SAN BASILIO DE PALENQUE.
Fundador de Palenque en el año 1603
Asesinado el 16 de Marzo de 1621 en Cartagena de Indias6

Additionally, a second, much smaller pedestal appeared next to the monument. Its surface announces: “Palenque: primer pueblo libre de América” (“Palenque: first free people of America”). In this way, and as to avoid any confusion, Palenque and its hero are clearly distinguished with their respective pedestals. Nonetheless, though written on stone, these most recent modifications did not last. Today, the commemorative plaque has been removed, and the secondary pedestal has been chiseled, as shown in figure 7.

Since its installation, the monument, and particularly its epigraph, has been a site of contestation. The successive rewritings of the epigraph sought to reframe the memorial as a symbol of liberation, independence, and maroon autonomy; but ultimately, Benkos’s distressing portrait seems to make it unattainable (see figure 8).

Placed on site in 1997, Benkos’s monument has been the site through which Palenqueros/as have dealt with the dialectics of slavery and freedom that hover over their historical identity and its representations. Since the memorial’s installation, the community has been incessantly modifying it, tinkering with its sculptural rhetoric and, through it, a White criollo interpretation of history, memory, and Black freedom. Thus, the collective sculpting that takes place in Palenque invites us to seek an understanding of freedom that does not depend on slavery to define itself.

Figure 7. The monument with its new inscription.

Figure 8. The last iteration of the monument. On its left side we see a smaller pedestal with a broken inscription. Here one can easily see what is left of the original chains. Photo: Google Earth.

One may ask: If a representation of freedom cannot be found here, in the monument of the mythical cimarron, where can it be found in Palenque? While I cannot respond for the Palenqueras and Palenqueros themselves, I believe that the photographs taken by Richard Cross during his time in Palenque during the mid-1970s—that is, twenty years before UNESCO’s recognition—open a path away from Benkos Biohó’s monument, to explore this particular question. Richard Cross accompanied Nina de Friedemann on her trips to Palenque from 1975 through 1977, while she was writing her groundbreaking study Ma Ngombe: guerreros y ganaderos. Although mostly limited to an academic audience, Cross’s photographs are probably the first images of Palenque to gain ample circulation. His photos also show aspects of Palenque beyond its much-lauded musical and culinary traditions—for example, he portrays children and women practicing boxing on various occasions, a playful remnant of training in wartime. Cross’s photographs help us think beyond the monument, far from the folkloric, amiable, and pacified representation of Palenque by UNESCO and the Colombian state.

Figure 9. “Children Playing in the Cemetery,” San Basilio de Palenque. Photo by Richard Cross, 1977.

In this photo, women and children are gathered around the tombs and niches, watching the boxing match on the street (see figure 9). They use the Kasariambé (cemetery) structures as physical platforms to better view the match or simply to rest against. No additional wall or marker divides the space of play from that of circulation (the street) or that of final rest. This is not to say that these dimensions are mixed up in Palenquero culture; on the contrary, their rich and complex funerary rituals carefully demarcate how, when, where, and for how long the living interact with the dead. But the photograph shows that these distinctions do not necessarily translate to the built environment in a definitive way; here, the cemetery is not exclusively for the dead.7 “Children Playing in the Cemetery” captures a corporeal familiarity of Palenque’s people with the space of death and its monuments. This scene would likely never take place in a Western cemetery.

More importantly, “Children Playing in the Cemetery” sheds light on an experience with monuments free from the chains of representation. Because who can say the children are not playing with the dead or for the dead? Today, Palenqueros and Palenqueras affirm without hesitation that the dead are with the living. Cross captured them all: the living partaking with the ghosts, enjoying the game, gossiping, sweating. The living and the spirits in a common retreat, which we could call mourning—or perhaps remembering. Children playing in the cemetery, or enjoying the freedom to remember on their own terms.

In stark contrast with the individual heroism that Vallejo’s sculpture celebrates, de Friedemann’s Ma Ngombe emphasizes that communitarian organization is primordial to Palenque. Hence, we could think of Benkos as a collective subject, mainly because maroonage is an alternative form of government to the State.8 Not by chance, the author repeatedly compares the Palenquero way of life to that of guerrillas.9 Ma Ngombe describes a very different Palenque from the one portrayed by UNESCO, which has aestheticized the town, pacifying its warrior ethos through the celebration of its cultural exceptionalism. The sculpture of the enslaved leader is the unmistakable sign of this neocolonial gesture.

From this standpoint, one might view the multiple alterations to the monument as ways in which Palenqueras and Palenqueros are helping Benkos to transition into local memory and collective ownership. Acts of defacement that nonetheless preserve the myth. We might interpret the incessant edits to the epigraph and the bust’s chains as a sculpting process: adding, removing, and chiseling are all anonymous gestures mobilized by remembering as a communal practice of resistance. A practice that puts into question the Criollo (Hispanic) representation of Black freedom, and the supposed solace of a language that settles and silences. And in this sculpting process, the community is telling a story—because, in Palenque, death always gives rise to the telling of stories.

A monument is a historical text, in the sense that it offers a path for questioning history. In the case of Benkos’s monument, this pathway is far from linear, cohesive, and unifying; rather, it behaves like a Borgesian maze, “a labyrinth of labyrinths [. . .] one sinuous spreading labyrinth that would encompass the past and the future and in some way involve the stars.” The monument’s winding path takes us from maroon warfare in the seventeenth century to the spectral remnants of Western colonialism. So, it might be worth asking, is an enchained Benkos the symbol of a unified Palenquero consciousness? The successive alterations to the body of the monument over the years seem to suggest that, in contradiction of Gideon’s “Nine Points of Monumentality,” unification is not the operating criterion when it comes to maroon freedom. Benkos’s monument in Palenque makes us wonder if it is not precisely in the modifications themselves that maroon freedom models its monumentality. A monument of freedom is not a stable representation but its constant displacement and negotiation; a monument of freedom is not unified but dispersed: It is free.

Ultimately, a monument is an effort to settle history and come to terms with its weight. But a maroon monument is not settled, nor is it a monument to unsettlement. A maroon monument has a “query with history,” as Glissant once put it. Benkos Biohó’s monument, then, is a matter of unsettlement. At the same time, monuments are essential because they help humans remember and mourn, and this is how Palenqueros link a vanished past and a future yet to come. However, in their case there is not just one linkage between “the past” and “the future,” but an incalculable multiplicity of returns. Cross’s photo shows that Palenqueros have a singular relationship to monuments. It is intimate, pragmatic, youthful, and, from a Catholic perspective, desacralizing. In other words, theirs is a ludic relationship to memory. Why would their relationship to Benkos’s monument be any different?

Maroonage isn’t keen on nostalgia; it is, however, inseparable from the madness of freedom. An urgency that we can hardly imagine today. San Basilio de Palenque is a monument; a patrimony of humanity; a “cultural space,” a living museum. However, one must ask, is it also a place to experience freedom’s collective force? Or are we doomed to contemplate only its representations?

One shouldn’t assume that the “identity constraints” certain institutions have deployed over Palenque exhaust its complexity or reveal the secrets of a pre-packaged maroonage. In other words, Palenque’s cultural reproduction of itself does not render Palenke fungible. Because here, freedom goes beyond the master/slave dialectic cast in the monument. Here, freedom is as unassuming as the Palenquero way of living. Of experiencing time, of expressing joy, of celebrating death. Freedom in spite of recognition.

1. Luis Guillermo Vallejo Vargas is the author of two of the most recognized historical monuments in Colombia: the “Monument to the Colonizers,” in which he evokes colonization in Antioquia and the Caldas, and the “Monument to the Comuneros” in Santander, which commemorates the Comuneros Revolution and its leader, José Antonio Galán. ↩

2. For more details on this, see Ferrari, “Un epígrafe cimarrón para la libertad.” ↩

3. This is not just the sculptor Fernando Vallejo’s figuration. It is also the vision of the sponsor, UNESCO’s program “La ruta del esclavo,” which seeks to identify and mark sites of Black resistance and liberation. On more than one occasion, the program’s aesthetics have recurred to allegories of the slave ship to represent Black emancipation; Benkos’s memorial is not the only one. In Guinea-Bissau’s monument of independence, we see a Brutalist reconstruction of the slave ship. The same happens in the recent UNESCO memorial “The Arc of Return.” ↩

4. “Palenke Founded by Benkos Bioho in 1603.” Author’s translation. ↩

5. “Benkos Bioho founder of Palenque. 1603” Author’s translation. ↩

6. “Benkos Biohó was born in the second half of the sixteenth century in the region of Biohó, part of the Bijangós Islands in Portuguese Guinea (now Guinea-Bissau), in western Africa. Benkos Biohó, also known as Domingo Biohó, was a leader who commanded a rebellion of enslaved maroons in the New Kingdom of Granada in the seventeenth century. Becoming the GREATEST HERO of the FIRST FREE PEOPLE of America SAN BASILIO DE PALENQUE. Founder of Palenque in 1603. Killed on March 16, 1621, in Cartagena de Indias.” Author’s translation. ↩

7. Maybe it is because the souls of the departed are not there anymore. They have already transitioned to the other world, and what’s left there are just the corporeal remains. Victor Simarra once explained to me that after a certain time, tombs were opened and cleaned to make space for new bodies. The remains were then placed in a secondary burial site. ↩

8. De Friedemann built her argument using, among others, Arrázola’s Palenque: Primer Pueblo Libre de América. The book compiles extensive documentation from the Archivo de Indias on rebel groups and their fortifications or “palenques” found in the region of the Montes de María, Colombia. According to the author, the threat of maroon warfare did not end with agreements such as the Entente Cordiale in 1713. He even registered insurgent plans in 1799 to enter Cartagena, take San Felipe Castle, and “murder the whites.” (Ma Ngombe, 56) ↩

9. Here it is important to note that de Friedemann is writing during the 1970s in Colombia, a critical moment for the guerrilla movement in the country. Ma Ngombe came out in November of 1979, when M-19 took the Palace of Justice. ↩

item.title: When Crimea Was Still a Place of Light
item.content:encoded:
When Crimea was still a place of light,
when gulls
were free
of orders,
when sandals
beat light
on the border
of water,
and gulls were the only patrols in the sky;
when women in bright dresses
walked barefoot or in cheap sandals,
in sandals, in sandals
instead of boots,
before missiles.
Before missiles,
I, too, loved it all.

item.title: Abyss and Rupture
item.content:encoded:
A late morning in June, biology class and dust, oozing by outside of time. Tiny specks of dust hang motionless, startlingly visible in the thick air. We take notes diligently, but without enthusiasm, barely following the movement of the chalk between Sister Weronika’s thin, wrinkled fingers. And it goes something like this:

Animals reproduce asexually or sexually and their young reach maturity as a result of their embryonic development, which can be either simple or complex. In simple embryonic development, there are no larvae and the juvenile stage mirrors the adult stage in miniature. In complex development, there is a larval stage and maturation brings about significant changes in their exterior and interior structure.

We doodle in the margins, clumsily drawing those larvae, pupae, and butterflies on the gridded pages of our notebooks. Life comes into existence, round and round, the cycles of development roll on, life after life and then the bell, finally! Uplifted by its ringing, we jog through the doors, around the bend in the corridor, down the stairs, and through the courtyard, straight to the ridge. Over and over, we ask each other, and ourselves:

“What eats ladybugs?”

“And what do ladybugs eat?”

And we laugh ourselves to tears, giggling until we’re out of breath. The summer we’ve been waiting for endlessly oozes by, always Friday, whole legions of Fridays, during which nothing ever happens. In those days, we sat in the weeds, in the tall grasses, grooming the earth of worms, caterpillars, and fat, repulsive larvae that we threw down the too-small shirts of anyone we happened not to like.

It’s June and we’re sitting on the ridge, fiddling with our phones, waiting for who knows what and whispering: Is this it? We shove currants, strawberries covered in an eiderdown of mold, and cherries, with their pink, sweet meat, out of sweaty plastic bags and straight into our mouths. We spit the pits at the boys, the stupid and the pretty ones. Spit-wet cigarettes pass from mouth to mouth, filters shimmering in the sun like glitter. The summer lives inside us for good now. We peel flakes of skin off each other’s arms, calves, and thighs; our faces are covered in cakey powder, stolen from our mothers. And we don’t know anything about ourselves at all, under the sunburned skin, under the powder and glittering lip gloss, under the pimples we pop in secret, versions of us that we don’t know lie in wait, and we don’t even think about what it will be like not to recognize them. By definition, we come in the plural, in sets, in gangs and packs, like eggs laid by butterflies in the grooves of tree bark; we—cast into the world in the middle of nowhere, foolish, helpless bodies, wanting the impossible.

***

A stream of days flowed past, in the shadow of the rupture: In the morning we saw each other at school, sat next to each other at our desks, shoulder to shoulder, then again later, shoulder to shoulder, we stood against the wall during breaks; stood in total silence, uneasy stillness. Back to our desks, back to the wall—and then the bell, then end, see ya, see ya. And then we could part, each going their own way to do their own thing. I had some stuff going on of course, but everything became empty and colorless then—abyss and rupture—and the only thing that interested me was analyzing Kinga’s behavior, all her gestures, dissecting them down to their smallest parts.

Kinga was in a stupor, yet also full of nervous energy. I watched furtively each time she reached for her phone, glanced at it, and put it down again, her red nails tapping the same two words on the small keyboard again and again: “Not yet.”

So she didn’t get it yet. She was still late. It seemed absurd to me. I had imagined a person in this state differently, a person who was pregnant, but here was the same Kinga, maybe a little quieter, a little paler. A burning red blush spread across her nose and cheeks when she caught those furtive glances of mine. We were silent.

Our school is on a small elevation. Leading uphill is a thin sidewalk full of holes that runs alongside a cobblestone street, stones that remember things no one else knows anymore. Tires roll lazily over the road, a steady rattle, the soundtrack to our silence, all the things that I don’t say out loud as we walk this small stretch of road together.

At the end of the sidewalk, the road splits in two. One way leads to what you might call downtown—the ungainly heart of every small place, the market square, where residents can take in the results of those European Union subsidies. The renovated facades bask in the sun, the benches shine with new paint, flowerbeds burst forth with violets and geraniums, and the old sidewalk panels have been replaced with blue-pink pavers. The other way strongly resists these developments, streets full of old houses, cottages really, and rotting fences with skinny cats stretched across them. Yards full of construction materials, rusty pails, old shoes, rakes. Greenery, best without any lame attempts at intervention, in its crazed late spring growth; low trees and dirt stained with the red splotches of fallen, splattered fruit. Moths and wasps, steadily buzzing, circle those splotches in a frenzy.

We always intuitively chose one of the ways, a little closer to home for one of us or the other, but it doesn’t matter either way, because it meant more time together. That was until all this dark stuff happened—recently it was just a gruff see ya and that was it, we turned around and went on with our afterschool lives, suddenly completely separate.

But today out of nowhere Kinga grabs me by the hand, a little too hard, and tells me to follow her. She takes me a different way, someplace completely different, turning into one side street and then another, passing more hedges, metal gates, and wire fencing. Kinga stops in front of one of those blocky houses, insulated with styrofoam. She gives me a questioning look and then reaches out for the bell at the gate, only to pull her hand back again and put it in the pocket of her cropped sweatshirt. She takes out a packet of cigarettes, red, strong, the longer ones this time.

“Want one?”

“Nah.”

“Maybe we could go to my place for a bit and talk?”

She sighs heavily, turns on her heel and walks two steps ahead of me. All of a sudden I feel how hot it is today, how hot and stuffy. The cars kick up dust, which floats high above our heads, muggy and dirty June air that sticks to your skin, slows you down. I can’t keep up with Kinga. Her broad shoulders take up the whole space between the curb and the netting, fences, and gates—all I see is Kinga’s back. Her back, like a wall topped with barbed wire. Safety, or the most terrifying of adventures; I watch the uncanny shimmer of her hair across that enormous yet tiny, girlish back, the sun hiding in its strands.

Kinga turns the key with precision and care. Daria is sleeping. Their mother is sleeping off the nightshift. So as usual we enter on our tiptoes, quietly, as quietly as possible. Kompot is cooling in a pot on the stove, frozen cherries, beautifully red. We pull the soft fruits right out of the pot with our hands and put them in our mouths still warm, at once sweet and tart. The velvet flesh and rough pits rub first against our tongues, and then our palates.

“I talked with Zocha, you know which one,” Kinga says reluctantly and spits a pit in the sink, good aim. The pit goes down the drain with an echo, clinking against the pipes for a moment before, poof, vanishing forever. I already know the weight of this story.

“I talked with Zocha and she confirmed that everything she told us that time wasn’t a lie, or some drunken delusion. It was all true and she told me everything.”

Everyone knows Zocha, the beloved example of parents and teachers—you don’t wanna learn? Fine by me, you’ll end up like Zocha, just wait. But Zocha didn’t end up so bad. I mean, she wasn’t even close to her end, she was only two or three years older than us. She did get thrown out of school for skipping class and talking back. Then she worked different gigs, serving at weddings, selling strawberries and blood-red currants at the market, cleaning for people. Lately she was in the city a lot, learning to do hair at night school, but what do I know, who cares.

During one of those winter house parties, we ended up in the bathroom with Zocha, or more specifically above Zocha. We were holding back her shiny red hair and rubbing her back in solidarity as streams of vomit, gray-red waterfalls, poured out of Zocha’s mouth. Classic. The terrible coughing echoed off the bathroom tiles.

“I poisoned myself, I poisoned myself,” Zocha lamented. And we just glanced at each other and shrugged.

“Everything will be okay Zocha, you’ll feel better soon.” We were on our way out, bored with this performance, which we’d already taken part in so many times before, in various configurations.

Then Zocha started howling. It was the howl of a dying animal. We sat right back down on the cold floor. We looked at Zocha tenderly—her face sticky with tears, drops of sweat on her forehead, vomit at the corner of her lips, twisted into a terrible grimace—

“Girls, I killed the baby . . . I killed the baby that was inside me.”

Kinga didn’t say anything. I understood, because bathrooms themselves absorb those kinds of sordid stories best. After all, girls have plenty of those. You hear all kinds—the uncle who was too eager to hold her on his lap and then squeezed her tight like that for half her childhood, someone’s mother who liked throwing her out of the house, probably without cause, and definitely without warning. And of course friends, or so-called friends, there’s always plenty of that type, who take and don’t give anything in return. And then you’re left alone with all that, all alone. Deal with it.

We had managed to become numb to it already, not probing too deeply into what was true, or half-true, or the source of gossip about this or that person. As long as it didn’t affect us, we left it alone—well, let it happen, bad luck comes for each of us in the end.

“Don’t worry, these kinds of things happen,” Kinga said.

And then we almost, almost made it out. I practically had my hand on the doorknob when Zocha sobbed: “Girls, am I a bad person?”

“Not at all, Zocha, you’re not. Things just happen sometimes, you know? Relax, get yourself together now, look, here’s some water, take the glass, drink.”

And with the glass in her hand—again, a flood, but of words instead of vomit: It wasn’t about the baby, God rest its soul, though Zocha wasn’t sure she believed in that, but okay that wasn’t the main problem here. Okay, so what’s the issue? Tell us Zocha, but make it quick, just give us the short version, we replied. It’s getting late and we have school in the morning, class at eight. You know how it is.

As it turned out, Zocha’s issue was her own good humor. That she got knocked up, that was less crucial now. She took one test, two, three—two lines every time, a slap in the face, like someone smacked her across the mouth, she said. And here she kind of lost the thread of the story, it fell to pieces that didn’t quite fit back together. As if there was something she didn’t want to tell us. She only said what she had imagined, some kind of sharp instrument, forceps, dingy basements, shady characters, but that it was actually much less scary than that. Her stomach hurt a little, maybe. That was it, and then it was all over. But now she had to go on living and every so often she was reminded of it. You probably know what that’s like, right?

It’s always the worst timing though. Like right now.

“Am I a bad person? I ask myself every so often,” Zocha said. “Because it’s not like I actually feel guilty. Honestly? I didn’t even feel sad, just relief, relief. I felt relieved, like I could breathe normally, my head full of ordinary things, you know: what I wanted to buy myself, what I wanted to eat. Everything was back to normal. And every so often I look inside myself, at this relief, and something isn’t right, because how could it be? I made the decision, okay, it happened, I took care of it, but I always thought that it would shake me up later, that I would be flooded with despair, you know, that I would be face down crying, until there was nothing left of me, just memories of the girl that I used to be, fragments of my life. And that would be my punishment. But that didn’t happen, nothing happened, I feel good, honestly, probably better than ever. I guess you probably can’t tell right now. Girls, tell me please, honestly now: Am I a bad person?”

I looked over at Kinga and I couldn’t tell if she was freaked out or just impatient. She looked like she was just playing with her hair or tapping her fingers against the cold floor tiles, but every so often she threw a searching look in Zocha’s direction.

“Zocha, you’re not a bad person, this is just what the world is like and we have to manage somehow, right?” Kinga said. “So drink some water, try to drink three glasses, chug them, all in one go. We have to go, okay?”

Mwah, a kiss on the top of her head, bye-bye, that was the finale of the bathroom scene starring Zocha. But as it turned out, there was another act, as I would now find out, which happened without me or my participation, thanks very much.

When Kinga realized what could be happening, she simply decided to prepare herself for various possibilities.

“In the meantime I wanted to be ready for the worst-case scenario, you know? If the shit hit the fan. It just happens that way, you’re just left alone with it all and you have to deal,” she says to me.

But when? Well, a couple of days ago she went to the thrift shop after school. Zocha had been working there for a while, and she told her that she had a time-sensitive problem, that she’d tell her everything out back. Was it right of her to say that she was pregnant by her brother—probably not. But Zocha took it well somehow and believed her, which is weird since her brother was a church-going—a married—man, a young dad, just had his third kid. But okay, that was Kinga’s charm, her lip didn’t twitch telling the worst lies—the only important thing was that Zocha agreed that it couldn’t happen this way and that she was ready to help if need be.

“But promise me that you won’t tell anyone. First of all it’s illegal in our country, so this is serious, swear to me on your family or on whomever, whatever, is most important to you. Swear on me.”

I swore.

The story was so straightforward, so ordinary, so clear. Without plot twists, subplots, or dark characters—just normal life. Zocha had a contact from somewhere, not important, and she could tell her later, if need be. She just went to this lady and not even in the big city. Here near us. They talked a bit and she asked her: what, when, and how. Good thing it was so early, because farther along she wouldn’t be able to help. Sure, Zocha had to pay. It cost her, but not much. She got two or three pills, she didn’t remember, and she took one first, and then she was supposed to wait several hours, maybe the whole day, maybe longer, and then take the second one. She bled heavily, her stomach hurt, and she wanted to throw up. She had a low fever. She said it sounded worse talking about it than it actually was, it was tolerable even. At home she said that she got a stomach bug from the girls at the restaurant where she was waitressing. But it wasn’t always like that, the lady told her, girls react to it differently, some really badly, which rarely happened, but it was important to call an ambulance and say that you were bleeding, that you think you’re having a miscarriage. They can’t do anything about that, maybe they say something under their breath, but fuck that, the important thing is that you get help. But anyways that barely ever happens and usually everything goes pretty okay.

That’s what Zocha told Kinga, that it was pretty okay, not pleasant, obviously.

“I would prefer not to go through all that, you see,” she says, blanching. And I recognize that blanching, that apprehension, the quiet before the storm. I’d only seen that storm once—Kinga crying, that tempest, thunder and hail, a storm that took Kinga over completely, possessed her.

“Okay, but if it’s not that bad, why are you so stressed about it? You seem so unhappy,” I ask Kinga. But Kinga doesn’t answer. I watch her press her fingers against the countertop, her knuckles turning white and her lips trembling. A painful grimace crosses her face, a wave of folds and furrows. Empty eyes, like a doll’s, covered in a film, glassy.

“Oh, come on Kinga . . . ”

She cries, cries, a perfected silent cry, a stream of tears falling from her eyes.

“Because I have the same thing Zocha had, the same thing, you know,” Kinga says to me in a whisper. “Like I’m only thinking about my guilt, my stupidity, my naivete, my lack of respect for school and the Church. And for my mom most of all, for my mom and Daria, about how she’d get punished too, they’d get it too. There won’t be any pieces left to pick up, however it ends, and in some ways it’s already begun, you see? This is the beginning, and some kind of ending to all this is inevitable.”

“I don’t understand.”

“I’m scared,” Kinga says even more softly. “I’m scared and if I don’t get my fucking period I’ll have to tell Marcin and that’s the worst part. Because if he says that it has a part of him too and he has a say in the decision, then I’ll have to take this on, give over my body rent-free and take care of everything, everything. Just like my mother, doing charity work for future generations. And if he says no, get rid of it? Then that’s even worse because it means that he doesn’t want me, that everything between us was a lie and I’ll have to confront that, kill all the butterflies in my stomach with one spritz of bug spray. And that’ll break my heart.”

I could have said to Kinga: Listen carefully, if you’re going to give yourself to someone, it’s best to do it in installments, bit by bit, and even better if it’s only the pieces you know you aren’t going to need later. Because it’s not a loan but a present, a gift, with nothing expected in return. Promise me, and yourself, swear, that if it comes to that then you’ll ration yourself out as militantly as possible. I could have told her that. I could have told her a lot of things, but I’m a teenager, so what do I know about life? Not a whole lot. I just rub her shoulders.

“Don’t worry Kinga, everything will be okay.”

Kinga sobs.

“How do you know?” she asks me, sobbing. A murmur from between her lips, almost as if she’s about to giggle, Kinga’s laugh, but no—it’s just the start of more tears.

They run profusely, an abundant flow that spills off the table and onto the floor—here’s a top-off of tears for you, a huge wave growing inside Kinga. The salty puddle of water grows and grows on the linoleum, and I say: “Kinga, stop, we’re gonna drown in here.”

I should take Kinga to the bathroom now, carefully dry her off with the hot stream of air from the hairdryer, hang her over the bathtub and if that doesn’t help, take her to the balcony and clothespin her to the laundry lines hanging under the ceiling. The wind would dry all of Kinga’s tears, sweep away this flood—and with it all of those problems, anxieties, all these issues which have now colored our lives, lives that were, up to this point, good. 

“What is it, girls?” Kinga’s mother’s voice rips me out of my thoughts. She moves silently, too, schooled in caring for a child with disabilities. She shoots suspicious looks at me, Kinga, and the table covered in tears, snot, and a mountain range of crumpled tissues.

“I think what’s going on here, if I know anything, is that Kinga is obsessed with some, pfft, boy, right? Let it out Kinga, cry long and hard until you’ve got nothing left. There’s no tears, no pain or broken heart or other such nonsense, that can compare with the suffering that a man will bring you when you let him share your life. Why are you looking at me like that? Do you see your father, Kinga? No, you don’t. But you see Daria. You see her every day. There’s your answer.” 

We stay quiet. She opens the fridge and takes out a metal bowl—giblets, livers, chicken feet and hearts—and washes them one by one under the sink. She pulls slimy blue veins out of them and rips off chunks of cartilage and bone with her nails and then throws them into the trash bin under the sink. Splat. Small drops of dirty red goo land on the floor.

“Don’t like it, don’t eat it. Up to you.”

***

Kinga leaves the house with me.  We walk the long way to the edge of town, where a huge meadow stretches out before us, the horizon marked by treetops, the beginning of the forest. A storm had been building all day, but never came, and instead there is a burst of color: the rays of the setting sun coloring the air copper-gold, the warmth of June. I take deep breaths of that vibrant air.

We sit on the arms of a broken-down bench and a sense of peace comes over us, an ocean of peace. We watch the wind tug at the poppies, their delicate blood-red petals, the cornflowers swaying. The grass plays like a harp, bees busily circling patches of daisies and clover, their little legs covered in pollen.

Now, in the quiet, the sun setting, the wind rocking the flowers, Kinga lets out a strange sigh, she bends forward and puts her hand down her pants, her whole palm pressed under the waist of her jeans, and gives me a long, curious look.

“Whaaat? Kinga?”

She pulls her hand out and sticks it in my face. Kinga’s palm and fingers are smeared with bloody slime.

“Look I got it! I got it!!!” Kinga shouts. Everything collapses as she screams, the flower stems wilt and fall into the meadow, birds fly off, as do soft, parachuting dandelion seeds, bark crumbles off the trees. And that handful of bad days, those tremorous anxieties—everything breaks apart into tiny pieces. That whole world, taken from us by force, will be returned to us after all, and it might even be a little better, more carefully put together, I think to myself.

“God, sorry, but I have to tell Marcin right away. Shit, maybe I’ll just go over there instead of calling, it’s not far.”

She gets ready to go, wiping her blood-smeared fingers on the grass, wiping blood on the moss.

So we won’t be celebrating together, celebrating this return to normalcy. Rupture, after all.

Mwah, mwah, I say goodbye to Kinga and then I’m home and the whole palette of colors that was just before my eyes melts into bland monochrome. I’m alone.

item.title: The Watchlist: August 2026
item.content:encoded:
From Other Press | Your Presence Is a Danger to Your Life: Voices of Survival and Witness in Gaza by Samar Yazbek, translated from the Arabic by Leri Price | Nonfiction | 336 pages | ISBN 9781635426120 | US$17.99

What the publisher says: “In Your Presence Is a Danger to Your Life—a title adapted from one of the flyers dropped on the residents of Gaza minutes before a bombing—Yazbek captures the raw, chilling accounts of ordinary civilians aged 13 to 65, who have witnessed what history may remember as one of the most savage military offensives of our time.”

What Buzz says: “One fine thread through this work is the persistence of hope, and therefore resistance. Miraculously, the testimonies leave little room for hatred: instead, they focus on mourning the dead, preserving memory, and finding the strength to overcome unimaginable brutality.”

What I say: These testimonies from Palestinians living in Gaza are important reading; the cumulative effect of encountering them in one place is also utterly devastating. The people whose voices we read come from a wide variety of backgrounds, but many of their experiences are similar, including grievous wounds, amputated limbs, and the shocking deaths of friends and family. Several chapters come to haunting conclusions, including these words from Isra Muhanna: “We have inherited war and pain and oppression over the decades, and now we are living through genocide.”

 

From Graywolf Press | Range by Dorthe Nors, translated from the Danish by Caroline Waight | Fiction | 336 pages | ISBN 9781644454046 | US$18.00

What the publisher says: “How to navigate the human-made boundaries of a boundless universe? How to be a caretaker if you’re not a mother and stand apart in your communities? Gunn’s mind ranges over these questions as she splits firewood, walks the forest, solves equations, sits in hunting stands, lies in fields, and observes—the animals, the locals, the seasons, the stars, her memories.”

What Charlotte Wood at The New York Times says: “This is an obliquely composed novel of advances and withdrawals and buried clues, and the reader, like the astronomer, must patiently ‘observe, note, conclude.’ As you watch and wait you’re sometimes rewarded with a narrative burst of fiery activity, or a subtler, more beautiful afterglow of revelation.”

What I say: Range is a novel that juxtaposes the nuances of social relations within a small community with the grand scale of its protagonist’s chosen discipline, astrophysics. That makes for an intentionally dizzying novel at times; though the book is written in a realistic vein, it can require patience to glean certain characters’ motivations. It isn’t the outright novel of big ideas or academic drama that one might expect from a book about an astrophysicist, but it retains the qualities of both.

 

From Seven Stories Press | Silencio by Clyo Mendoza, translated from the Spanish by Christina MacSweeney | Fiction | 192 pages | ISBN 9781644215616 | US$18.95

What the publisher says: “Silencio tells the story of Águeda, a young woman mourning the death of her mother. When the townspeople deny her a grave in the local cemetery, the mother’s body vanishes. Águeda knows her father is hiding it, and when she confronts him, he punishes her defiance with confinement.”

What Publishers Weekly says: “The lyrical animism is juxtaposed with matter-of-fact journalistic accounts of Mexican women experiencing exploitation and heartache in the US. It’s difficult to piece together, but Mendoza transcends the grim material in countless beautiful passages. Patient readers and lovers of poetry will delight in this demanding but dazzling project.”

What I say: This sentence, which appears in the first third of Silencio, serves as a kind of thesis for the entire book: “There are houses that do this to you, that waft the heat of a dangerous idea to you, that overwhelm you.”  In focusing on a traumatized family with an abusive patriarch and sometimes extending outward into the lives of other people throughout Mexico, this narrative abounds with shocking violence and meditations on grief.

 

From Tripwire Editions | And death shall have no dominion / Killing “The Mother” by Victoria Guerrero-Peirano, translated from the Spanish by Honora Spicer | Nonfiction | 70 pages | ISBN 9798218855864 | US$12.00

What the publisher says: “Killing ‘The Mother’ charts death inside healthcare bureaucracy through brutal, surreal, and fragmentary poetic prose, grappling with the capitalist devastation of systems of social care and how writing might enact forms of conception in the face of such conditions. Victoria Guerrero-Peirano has been recognized as one of the most singular and powerful voices of contemporary Peruvian poetry.”

What Asymptote Journal says: “[E]ven at its most grim, Guerrero remains clinically attentive to the social and political forces that determine embodied experience, her oscillation between passion and restraint serving to heighten the eeriness of her prose.”

What I say: If you suspect that a book with part of its title struck through might involve some contradictions, you would be absolutely correct. In Honora Spicer’s translation, Victoria Guerrero-Peirano’s book abounds with shifting boundaries and identities: On its first page, you’ll find the paradoxical statement, “The poet was dead, but Victoria was still breathing.” There’s a religious quality to this book as well, with the objects photographed within taking on the status of relics. It’s a deeply personal narrative that frequently ventures into the archetypal.

 

From Astra Publishing House | The Shame is Over: A Personal History by Anja Meulenbelt, translated from the Dutch by Ann Oosthuizen | Nonfiction | 320 pages | ISBN 9781662603723 | US$22.00

What the publisher says: “First published in 1976, The Shame is Over blends a raw account of Meulenbelt’s evolution as a mother, lover, and political thinker with an incisive portrayal of the struggles women face in their pursuit of autonomy and equality. Meulenbelt doesn’t shy away from the internal tensions of the feminist movement—its contradictions, divisions, and emotional costs.”

What Publishers Weekly says: “After becoming pregnant at 16 in 1961, Meulenbelt was forced to leave school and marry her son’s father. She spent years in poverty after she divorced him at 19 to escape his abuse, and was subsequently drawn into left-wing activism in 1960s Amsterdam. The Marxist and Maoist groups she joined, which were dominated by men, talked of oppression but were blind to misogyny.”

What I say: Anja Meulenbelt’s The Shame Is Over is a nuanced look at its author’s own evolving political consciousness, along with her frustration with ideologies that don’t consider women’s lived experiences. (Of one such line of thinking, she wryly comments, “With a few words we have again been incorporated, made subservient to the class struggle.”) There’s also a metatextual element here, as Meulenbelt occasionally writes about various political parties’ reactions to her writing.

item.title: Heracleocene
item.content:encoded:
One time at our dacha, when we were little, my friends and I were told a story about a group of kids who played with a plant. They pretended that the plant’s stalk was a set of binoculars or a telescope. They burned their eyes. That’s how I learned about hogweed. That same year in our Russian language textbook we read a small text called “Hogweed.” The author praised the health properties of the plant, suggested making a little pipe out of its stalk. After you were done playing with it, the text advised, don’t throw the pipe out—take a bite. After all, a hogweed is “crunchy like a cucumber.” I couldn’t find the text in 2024, but I clearly remember how this text disturbed me, especially the comparison of hogweed to a cucumber. I didn’t know there were other, safer species, like the Siberian hogweed, the one presumably mentioned in the textbook. I was indignant. Our whole dacha was overgrown with Sosnovsky’s hogweed. Described in the 1940s and named by the botanist Ida Mandenova after her teacher, this species of hogweed was wrenched out of its native ecosystem in the Caucasus mountains, where it had its own place, and transplanted into a field for agrobiological experimentation. It was expected to help combat the post-war famine: the silage was to be fed to the cattle, the cattle fed to the humans, the humans fed to the totalitarian machine. But the hogweed escaped. Entering a cruel collaboration with the sun, it discovered its latent ability to burn our mucus membranes, our skin, our tongues. I have thought a lot about Sosnovsky’s hogweed. About how, after not harming anyone in its native area, it began destroying ecosystems and conquering territories. About how, due to climate change, coral reefs are bleaching away and vanishing, but the hogweed is moving on, blooming in languid umbrellas. About how, having been the victim of a failed experiment, it has forever become a flowerhead of coloniality, militarism, scientific ignorance, patriarchy, toxicity, and a monotony of form. I decided to imagine what the planet would look like when hogweed would finally conquer it all, establish its supremacy. I called this era Heracleocene (or “hogweedcene”). But I also decided not to give up on hope. Little space is given to hope, but for me it’s the most important aspect of this poem. I have been looking for hope in my search for this language.

 

lessons from the earth

under the lash

under the table

            from under the floorboards

from under the tomb

of authoritarian regimes

of totalitarian regimes

from under the mycelium

of actor-network theory

from under oil arteries

(ceci n’est pas une pipeline)

from under the putrid poison of organic languages

from under garbage; garbages

 

but also just: a handful of soil

on a plot of land

on this earth

unteaches the transport of speech

 

  ▪︎

 

children look at the cloud through a telescope

 

a telescope coated in furanocoumarins

children, don’t play with the furanocoumarins

don’t swallow magnifying equipment

 

time mutated into a burn

 

children play with a bruise in the mouth

with a fire on the tongue

item.title: The City and the Writer: In Jakarta with Khairani Barokka
item.content:encoded:
If each city is like a game of chess, the day when I have learned the rules, I shall finally possess my empire, even if I shall never succeed in knowing all the cities it contains.

—Italo Calvino, Invisible Cities

 

Can you describe the mood of Jakarta as you feel/see it?

Hypercapitalist monstrosities amidst unmappable jalan tikus (“rat lanes”); uncapturable masses; brawling, unresting, sonic pulse-scapes; sleaze and azan; laughter and fireworks; unending persistence of mothers of the disappeared; aches of resilience, in a city of quiet blows; slang unfurling and evolving; culinary magnetism all across the map; dangdut and hundreds of archipelagic languages, philosophies, and bodily rhythms echoing street vendors booming into uneven streets, sounding, sounding, sounding.

 

What is your most heartbreaking memory in this city?

Jakarta is a city of living heartbreaks, and the persistence that pours out of them. I felt this acutely as a child raised in this epicenter of Soeharto’s Western-backed, capitalist military dictatorship, in the aftermath of the 1965–66 genocide that affected our elders, who held their breaths and wrote their freedoms in subterfuge, and were asked to tell their children this mass murder had not occurred, just as they had been forced to deny it had occurred in their own childhoods. Resistance has always been there, despite what certain documentaries and books by Westerners on these atrocities will show you. And artists who have experienced unbearable things have always been creating. They are the ones who deserve to be heard the most.

 

What is the most extraordinary detail, one that goes unnoticed by most, of the city?

D/deaf and/or disabled people are everywhere in Jakarta, including people without what abled society sees as visible markers of disability, yet we are still underserved by our city’s infrastructures and attitudes; shifts are there, but are happening at too glacial a pace. Somewhere underneath are the spirits of indigenous disability justice cultures, asking us to keep living under grotesque discrimination, and to support each other.

 

What writer(s) from here should we read?

There are so many. Among my favorites to read in Indonesian are Ziggy Zezsyazeoviennazabrizkie, Intan Paramaditha, Cyntha Hariadi . . . While many wonderful writers such as Hanna Fransisca—who I find captures the comedic elements of the city so well—are originally from elsewhere, they are just as necessary to a literary understanding of Jakarta that includes vital migrant perspectives.

 

Is there a place here you return to often?

For me as a Minang person (often otherwise known as Padang), a trip to at least one of the innumerable traditional Padang restaurants is a must. Does my family cook and serve phenomenal forms of this culinary art in their homes? Yes, but it is only at a Padang restaurant that you see, under the gaze of illustrated icons in the shape of rumah gadang, the artfully stacked formations of plates holding each other up in the glass window, all the shared plates laid out in similar fashion on your table at the start of your meal, by service staff whose movements are shaped in some way by the sanctity of tari piring, and the practice of paying for only exactly how much is eaten from these shared receptacles.

 

Is there an iconic literary place we should know?

Taman Ismail Marzuki (TIM) has been a memory-making place for innumerable Jakartans across the arts, and there are plays, readings, films, art exhibitions, concerts, and late-night, post-show conversations in its food court that have stayed with us. In the cultural park you’ll also find the Jakarta Arts Institute (IKJ), and the Jakarta Planetarium; the energies of both together might have something to do with how the stars and damp earth feeding each other seem to me part of the place’s animus, and that of many works produced there.

There have been demonstration efforts by artists these past months against plans for “commercial revitalization” in the TIM complex, and they are well justified. This is a historic place whose future is under threat, and we’re hoping against hope that these potentially very destructive “development” plans don’t come to pass.

 

Are there hidden cities within this city that have intrigued or seduced you?

Jakarta is a city where so much of our lives are spent on the go; spending hours and hours (especially in the pre-MRT days) in or on vehicles. I find vehicle memories of a movable cityscape—watching the urban layout shape-shift over days, weeks, years, including routes and rat lanes—to be deeply imprinted.

The city Jakartans inhabit and create when we are in trains, buses, bajaj, or bemo, on ojek (motorcycle taxis), becak (cycle rickshaws, when I was very young, before they were sadly banned from city), and other moving objects is key to the vibrancy and kineticism that infects the rest of the landscape. The conversations you have when you are in an enclosed, moving space with other people, and are forced to stay in these spaces for an extended period, nurture relationships and humor, create frictions, resolutions. These are times when I have deeply felt like part of a collective. Every time I return, even if I’ve been there not so long ago, traversing the city I notice so many changes go by. Being in motion has allowed us to observe and remember those changes, to cement continually new forms of nostalgia.

 

Where does passion live here?

Where does it not? To me it is a city of messy emotions, difficult memories, fiery activism, of loving what may destroy us despite ourselves, and tricking it into laughing with us.

 

What is the title of one of your works about Jakarta and what inspired it exactly?

My book (and fourteen-year art project, of which the book is part) Annah, Infinite was shaped greatly by my late grandmother’s celebration of Javanese girlhoods, including through the black-and-white photos of her and her friends at the age of around thirteen that she kept in her Jakarta bedroom my whole life. It is, of course, juxtaposed with Gauguin’s vile exoticization in the painting Annah la Javanaise. The chapter “Nightmares of 1965” is both a memory of holding one’s breath as a result of colonial violence, and an exploration of the often undiscussed ways we experience art and family through the lens of what nervous systems can no longer hold inside.

 

Inspired by Levi, “Outside Jakarta does an outside exist?”

Outside Jakarta, over 700 cultures and languages exist in the archipelago, just as hundreds of them are present inside city limits, and native Jakartans, the Betawi people, bring their Jakarta with them wherever they go. Jakarta is a morass of energy and freneticism, where “outside” and “inside,” “outsider” and “insider” are continually blurred boundaries. The overdevelopment of the Jabodetabek area (Jakarta-Bogor-Depok-Tangerang-Bekasi) is a constantly tentacling sprawl. Begitulah kotaku.


Khairani Barokka is a writer, artist, arts consultant, and translator from Jakarta, now UK-based. Barokka’s work has been presented widely internationally, and centers disability justice as anticolonial praxis, environmental justice, and access as translation. She regularly lectures, judges, mentors, and consults for arts organizations, and has a PhD by Practice in Visual Cultures from Goldsmiths, University of London. She has been a UNFPA Indonesian Young Leader Driving Social Change, a Delfina Foundation Associate Artist, an Artforum Must-See, and the first non-British Associate Artist at the UK’s National Centre for Writing. She was the first Poet-in-Residence at Modern Poetry in Translation and became the magazine’s first non-British editor. In 2023, Barokka was longlisted for the Loewe/Studio Voltaire Arts Award, and shortlisted for the Asian Women of Achievement Awards in the Arts and Culture Category. Her commissions have included the ICA, Wellcome Collection, Jakarta Biennale, Southbank Centre, and Serpentine Galleries. Her most recent art exhibition was Kerokan Pol, four short films as part of a crip duo show/collaboration with Bella Milroy called “Languages of Intimacy,” curated by Grand Union and shown at Birmingham College of Art Gallery in October–November 2025. Her books include Indigenous Species (Tilted Axis), Stairs and Whispers: D/deaf and Disabled Poets Write Back (Nine Arches, as co-editor), Rope (Nine Arches), Ultimatum Orangutan (Nine Arches), shortlisted for the 2022 Barbellion Prize, and 2024’s amuk (Nine Arches), currently longlisted for the 2025 Jhalak Prize. Her speculative nonfiction debut, Annah, Infinite (Tilted Axis Press, 2025), was an Expert Pick in The Bookseller.

item.title: One Glance Is Enough for Us to Know: Three Poems
item.content:encoded:
And when the terrible times are behind us
and the years that we have lost
fall over the edge of the table one after another
and we look at each other: older now but with our limbs still intact
and our wishes which have not gotten any smaller

maybe we have been walking in circles
on a cinder track while gradually turning silent
me on the easier inner lane you on the outside looking at me
but now at the finish line one glance is enough for us to know
there was never any other choice for us but each other

 

We step into a still life from the seventeenth century
and strip off our clothes and I see in your reflection in the goblet
how beautiful you are—you make a bed for us
in the pure linen napkin behind the lobster’s claw
so we are safe from a viewer’s gaze
it is the bitterness of the white of the lemon’s peel
curled into a spiral of fruitless waiting
that is left for us once Eternity has set us free again
and we look sadly into the petrified stare of the animal
whose claws lie before us in fossilized longing
nothing has gotten any better as we gather up our things
and sheepishly step back out of the painting

 

Apparent Magnitude

if we could banish the shock waves
of the last years to the night sky could
name the flaring stars the un-
discovered patterns of our astonishment about
what is possible what gets said what doesn’t
happen if we could arrange everything we consider
monstrous into constellations would we
still be who we once were: people who
gaze at the heavens and hope and wish and love?

item.title: Women in Translation Month 2026: WWB Staff Picks
item.content:encoded:
For Women in Translation Month, my book recommendation will be The Sleep Thief. It’s Ibtisam Azem’s first novel and it’s a slim, dreamlike book about a Palestinian man, Gharib, whose name means “the stranger,” and a few days. I really like how lyrical and gently experimental the book is. It’s been translated from the Arabic by Sinan Antoon, who’s also a poet.

—Sohini Basak, Poetry Editor

 

In an Albanian mountain village ruled by ancient law, a young woman’s decision triggers a cascade of bloody violence that rips apart her family and shatters several lives. Torn between an unwanted arranged marriage and her forbidden passion for a female friend, Bekija chooses to become a sworn virgin, renouncing all claims to femininity to live as a man. Rene Karabash’s poetic stream of consciousness, in Izidora Angel’s dazzling translation, conveys the swirling themes of identity, queerness, ritual, and freedom. She Who Remains was published in February, just in time to be shortlisted for the International Booker Prize; I expect to see it leading the nominations for the US translation prizes this fall.

—Susan Harris, Editorial Director

 

I devoured this book! I love experimental biographies that incorporate memoir, and The Queen of Swords feels like a conversation across time between Elena Garro and Jazmina Barrera. Barrera stitches together fragments of Garro’s life, deliberately leaving loose threads and gaps exposed. We are left with more questions than answers, invited to commune with ghosts, with the contradictions and the uncertainties surrounding Garro’s life, and to sit with all its mystery.

—Alicia Lim, Finance and Operations Manager

 

Admittedly, I haven’t read it yet, but up next on my list is Yoko Tawada’s essay collection Exophony: Voyages Outside the Mother Tongue, translated by Lisa Hofmann-Kuroda. Tawada is a brilliant, funny author who writes in both Japanese and German, and I’m eager to see how she tackles the fascinating topic of transiting between languages. A few promising essay titles from the table of contents: “On Mistranslating the Moon” and “Los Angeles: The Poetic Ravine between Languages.”

—Nina Perrotta, Senior Editor and Development Manager

 

Here is a distilled, elemental collection that stages, with every poem, a life lived—thriving, attentive, defiant, tender—amid the ruins, in Palestine. “Enter” commences each title, theatrically: enter wrist pain, enter apartheid, enter girl with books. Translated nimbly by Elkamel, Taha’s ambition is encyclopedic, quotidian in its mise en scène: beauty jostles with suffering and devastation, olive trees and morning dew sit next to torturers, checkpoints, prisoners incubating philosophers. In those hills a universe starts and ends, “leaving no trace of this world / but the mystery of how it began.” Read this if you like Adania Shibli and Etel Adnan for their sparse, oracular precision; in Taha’s pages you will find an accounting, a dramatis personae of injustice, an eschatology heavy with the knowledge that another world is possible.

—Alex Tan, Editorial Fellow

 

The book that I’m most excited to read this Women in Translation Month is called Seeing Further by Esther Kinsky and translated from German by Caroline Schmidt. To me, there is no better summer activity than going on a hot summer day to sit in a cold, dark movie theater seeing a summer blockbuster. And so I’m really excited to dig into this book, which is about a woman who comes across a dilapidated movie theater in rural Hungary and takes on the very challenging task of trying to refurbish it. This might be the book for you if you are a cinephile, if you’re stubborn about changing technologies, or if you very strongly believe that the best way to see a movie is with other people.

—Maggie Vlietstra, Education Program Manager

 

Waist Deep is the perfect steamy novel to end your summer on. It’s the debut novel from Linea Maja Ernst, translated from Danish by Sherilyn Nicolette Hellberg, and it takes place at a Danish lake house in the summer. A group of friends from college reunite to catch up and reminisce, claiming that these are the people they’re closest to in the whole world even while they are on guard against one another’s real and imaginary judgments. There’s an element of A Midsummer Night’s Dream to it—a marriage, everyone in love with everyone else, an idyllic location. What I particularly loved was, in addition to lush prose and luxurious pacing that still feels watertight, that Ernst lovingly and lightly pokes fun at all kinds of millennial stereotypes and ways of being in, and looking at, the world. It’s one of the best encapsulations I’ve read of how it feels to try to be an engaged thirty- or forty-something at this point in world history while also longing to shed responsibilities altogether.

—Anna Claire Weber, Marketing & Communications Manager
